OpenAI Engineer Secretly Recorded Dozens of Meetings, Prosecutors Say
articles.description: A court filing said the engineer captured meetings on customers, A.I. safety and a foreign government briefing. Federal prosecutors are investigating what he did with the recordings.
articles.content: Prosecutors say former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan had hundreds of audio files, including dozens of OpenAI meeting recordings that may contain trade secrets, and uploaded some recordings to Dropbox. They’re opposing his release on bail. He has pleaded not guilty and denies stealing trade secrets for Saudi Arabia. His lawyers have sought a $1 million bond. US prosecutors opposing former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan’s release on bail say investigators found hundreds of audio files on his computer, including dozens of recordings of OpenAI meetings and conversations. Many involved “what may be trade secrets,” according to Engadget’s account of the filing. Source Alfozan has pleaded not guilty to all charges, the Financial Times reports. He denies stealing OpenAI trade secrets for Saudi Arabia, according to Engadget. His lawyers argue that the government has produced no evidence that he acted for Saudi intelligence, characterizing his actions as those of an “overly curious tinkerer without any more nefarious intentions”. SourceSource The FT reports that Alfozan faces a statutory maximum of five years in prison if convicted of unlawfully intercepting or attempting to intercept oral communication. Source According to the FT, prosecutors described more than 160 hours of recordings and alleged that Alfozan recorded dozens of meetings over three weeks in September. At least one recording captured a meeting between OpenAI and representatives of an unnamed foreign administration. Prosecutors also allege that he photographed a confidential term sheet between OpenAI and another company. Source “Evidence developed to date strongly suggests the defendant recorded many meetings that he had no authority to, and did not, attend and that he did so without notice to — let alone authorisation from — anyone at OpenAI,” prosecutors said, according to the FT. Source The alleged hardware was less futuristic than the setting: the FT describes a recording device wrapped in toilet paper and hidden behind a conference-room television. It was discovered during a routine sweep in September. Engadget reports that Alfozan was arrested in October and fired that same day. SourceSource Engadget reports that prosecutors say Alfozan uploaded some recordings to Dropbox and used AI to generate transcripts, organizing them by date and renaming them according to their contents. The reporting does not identify who else, if anyone, accessed those uploads. Source Prosecutors also alleged frequent communication with people affiliated with the Saudi government while arguing that Alfozan posed a flight risk, according to Engadget. Those alleged contacts alone do not establish that he worked for Saudi intelligence or transferred recordings to the government. SourceSource His lawyers have sought a $1 million bond. Engadget reported that a hearing on his request was scheduled for November 24 in San Francisco. SourceSource

articles.title: Fury in Congress over Huang’s reinstatement as lawmakers move forward with hearings
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — Members of Congress responded with swift, bipartisan fury Monday over the Nvidia board’s surprise decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang at the behest of President Donald Trump, opening a new phase of questions about the chipmaking giant and potential national security lapses. Sen. Tim Scott, the outgoing Republican chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, announced that Huang will testify publicly before the panel on Dec. 3. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair, said the Trump administration needs to explain what role U.S. officials played in what she called a “reckless” decision. Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump’s direct involvement with Nvidia’s decision-making “raises serious national security and corruption questions.” “We must investigate these actions,” said Garcia of California. Nvidia was already facing sharp scrutiny from Congress after Huang acknowledged a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. officials believed to be a spy. Putting Huang back in charge, after Trump said the board did “what we wanted them to do,” raised stark concerns over the administration’s role in the company that is central to the AI economy. As Democrats prepare to take charge of Congress in January, they are mounting investigations into the Trump administration, particularly Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has close ties with the company. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier this month said he was frustrated by the Commerce Department’s delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed, the company whose CEO, Alice Huang, was involved with Jensen Huang. “The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back,” said Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas, the Republican chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee. “Congress has much to investigate,” he said. Huang is expected to appear for two days of interviews with three House committees next week, along with his public hearing at the Senate panel. “The NVIDIA board’s brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed,” said a joint statement from Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chairman of the House Select Committee on China; Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., chairman of the House Intelligence Committee; and Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. “We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities.” Of concern to Congress is whether Nvidia, one of the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies, has been selling its chips to China, in violation of export controls as the U.S. tries to protect certain technology that is at the core of the AI race. Earlier this year, members of Congress urged the U.S. Commerce Department to “suspend or reconsider” Nvidia’s export licenses to China and to conduct a full national security review, according to a release earlier this month from Warren and a key Republican on the Senate banking committee, Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana. “Since then, NVIDIA has reportedly received approvals to export hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to China’s military, all while attempting to influence the debate over chip controls in Washington, D.C.,” they wrote in a statement in November. “NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang’s confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China’s intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer,” the two senators said. While Republican leaders were mostly quiet on Huang’s return to Nvidia, other Republicans spoke more forcefully Monday. Texas Sen. John Cornyn, who lost his seat after Trump endorsed his GOP primary opponent, questioned the company’s comment that the U.S. said there was no security risk. “No national security risk? Based on what?” Cornyn posted. Cornyn asked whether the FBI did a defensive briefing of Huang to conclude there was no risk, “If not, why not?” Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon wrote on social media that the U.S. cannot say it wants to win the AI competition and then give China its best technology. “Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high end computer chips sales to China,” wrote Bacon, who is retiring from Congress. Ahead of the announcement but after Trump’s call for Huang to be reinstated, Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga of Michigan, who lost reelection to a Democrat, posted: “Ummm… she was, and is, a spy. How about we get serious about making sure China doesn’t steal US company technology?” Utah Sen. John Curtis asked similar questions. “Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board?” Curtis asked. “And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?” Democrats are preparing to dive more deeply into questions of national security and political corruption in Washington as they take over the committee gavels in January. “The guy who was having an affair with a Chinese spy while working relentlessly to help China get access to as many AI chips as possible? Really?” posted Delaware Sen. Chris Coons, who is poised to become the chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee when Democrats take the majority. Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, a Democrat, said that Congress should investigate “what stock positions took place before the announcement.” Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, who will chair the Senate finance committee and serves on the Senate intelligence committee, said Huang’s restatement shows that under Trump and his administration, “our national security is for sale.” “In January, Democrats will hold this corrupt administration accountable,” Wyden said. Associated Press writers Kevin Freking, Aamer Madhani, Joey Cappelletti and Chris Rugaber contributed to this report.

articles.title: Sponsored Commentary: Immigrant talent powers the American economy
articles.description: At 1 a.m., logistics workers in Kentucky start the night shift at a fulfillment center, packing and loading boxes for morning deliveries. (Photo by Getty / Me 3645 Studio) At 4 a.m., farm workers in Iowa walk their cows to the milking parlor to produce dairy that will line grocery store shelves throughout the state. […]
articles.content: Business leaders have affirmed immigrants importance to the workforce due to increasing labor demands in areas such as construction, agriculture and care. (Photo by Getty / Maskot) At 1 a.m., logistics workers in Kentucky start the night shift at a fulfillment center, packing and loading boxes for morning deliveries. (Photo by Getty / Me 3645 Studio) At 4 a.m., farm workers in Iowa walk their cows to the milking parlor to produce dairy that will line grocery store shelves throughout the state. (Photo by Getty / Guillermo Spelucin) At 5 p.m., a chef in Minnesota opens the doors of her restaurant, relying on a team of servers, line cooks, runners, and dishwashers to make every guest feel at home. (Photo by Getty / FG Trade) At 9 p.m.,an overnight crew in North Texas begins placing traffic cones alongside Highway 75, closing lanes to begin critical maintenance on a route over 200,000 vehicles travel each day. (Photo by Getty / Portland Press Herald) On an average day in the United States, more than 30 million immigrants work around the clock to power our economy. Immigrants carry out thousands of essential services daily that keep America’s cities running, our families fed and our loved ones cared for. Today, 1 in 6 employees in the country is an immigrant, and their participation is even more pronounced in essential sectors such as construction and direct care, where they represent nearly 30% of the workforce. In the agricultural sector, that number leaps to 68%. These figures reflect more than just their labor participation. They demonstrate that the rights of immigrant workers are inseparable from the well-being of our nation as a whole. Yet, over the past decade, shifting immigration policies have made it harder for immigrants — many of whom have work authorization and are long-term members of our workforce — to contribute their talents to local economies. Even for those who can secure employment, a job rarely guarantees true security: Many face wage theft, unsafe working conditions and a lack of protections. This instability fuels anxiety among workers, who often see the risk of retaliation as far too high to advocate for their rights — and the harms extend far beyond the workplace. Estimates suggest milk prices could double without the immigrant workers who produce 79% of the country’s milk supply. They also make up nearly a third of the homebuilding workforce, critical for addressing the nation’s 1.5 million-home shortage. And the need for their skills is only going to grow: By 2030, older adults are expected to outnumber children for the first time in U.S. history, requiring 9.3 million care workers to handle the shift. Without immigrant care workers, families may be forced to reduce work hours or leave the workforce altogether to care for aging family members. An America without immigrant talent is an America with higher grocery prices and closed storefronts. It is a nation with construction delays and families struggling to juggle work and caregiving responsibilities. Perhaps that’s why some of the loudest proponents of long-term, quality employment for immigrant workers are employers themselves. The foundation of our economy A growing number of business leaders from across the country believe immigrants are a vital part of the solution to meet rapidly rising labor demands across multiple industries, including construction, agriculture and care. More than 1,700 employers and CEOs have come together as part of the American Business Immigration Coalition (ABIC), a Ford Foundation grantee, to support legal pathways for a thriving immigrant workforce. Its members include manufacturers, ranchers, nursing home owners and general contractors across states, all united in the belief that businesses have a responsibility to support immigrant workers. “It’s not easy waking up at 3 a.m. every day and milking a 1,500-pound animal,” said Rebecca Shi, CEO of ABIC. “It’s not easy to fix shingles on a roof in 110-degree heat with our climate getting hotter year after year. We have found that even when employers post wages that are three times higher than the local minimum wage, there aren’t many American-born workers waiting in line to perform this labor. Those who remain in these jobs are almost always immigrants.” For Shi, immigrants provide the foundation on which the broader economy sits. Far from displacing American-born workers, she noted that immigrant participation in the workforce helps grow the economy and create more jobs for all people in the U.S. Shi cited a restaurant as an example: “In a restaurant, immigrants are typically working the so-called back-of-house jobs — the dishwashers, the busboys, the sous chefs. Their labor creates the front-of-house jobs preferred by American-born workers — the host, the bartender, the manager. So when you lose the back of the house, that also means a reduction of jobs for American-born workers at the front of the house.” A way of living From her restaurant in St. Paul, Minnesota, chef and owner Karyn Tomlinson, an ABIC member, agreed: “I get all the fame and glory being up front, but I arguably have the least important job.” She opened Myriel in 2021, named after the bishop in “Les Misérables” who invites downtrodden Jean Valjean to a meal at his table and treats him with dignity despite his turbulent past. That ethos of hospitality animates the restaurant and has carried Tomlinson and her team to top honors, including a James Beard Award. As her kitchen began to prepare the staff meal ahead of their dinner service, Tomlinson talked about the impact immigrants have had on restaurants throughout the Twin Cities. She described the excitement they bring to their roles, their years of honed skills and their influence on other staff. “They raised the bar for my expectations of what we should all work like,” she said. As part of her job, Tomlinson spends a lot of time at local farms and witnesses how immigrant workers are the backbone of our food system, from planting and harvesting crops to packaging and delivering them to restaurants. “You can’t reschedule a harvest, so you need dependable, respected workers,” she said. “When you take those key players out of that picture, it impedes the whole system.” Once produce arrives in her kitchen, cooks of various cultural backgrounds find expression through the menu, from the Bulgarian-brined feta introduced by her chef de cuisine to the Vietnamese-inspired fish sauce her kitchen makes from catches reeled in from local lakes. Their impact on the restaurant “is like turning the lights up in a room,” Tomlinson said. And it is only through offering her employees the respect and dignity they deserve that a spirit of hospitality is able to extend from the back of the house to diners in the front. “If you’re treating each other well as a team, then your guests will see it — when the hospitality is not a performance, but a way of living,” she said. That is a formula not just for supporting staff, but for great service and successful storefronts. “If you want more thriving, good businesses, it needs to start with happy workers.” The work that makes all other work possible Felicia is the type of nanny who asks the kids she cares for what they would like to have for breakfast every day. “It’s always good to have the kids pick, so it opens up their appetite,” she said. Born the eldest of six children in the Caribbean, she spent much of her childhood raising her siblings, and knew once she arrived in the United States that she wanted to pursue a career in childcare. But for the first several years, her lack of permanent legal status meant Felicia (whose name and identifying details have been changed) lived in persistent fear of retaliation. Unaware of her rights, Felicia tended to families who demanded long hours without overtime pay and housekeeping in addition to childcare. Her time as a nanny hit a low while caring for the children of a man in Queens whose unreasonable demands and disrespect for her needs led to a period of overwhelming stress. It bled into her childcare; when she took the children in her care to the playground, she kept to herself. One day in the park, Felicia was approached by a nanny who was a member of the National Domestic Workers Alliance (NDWA), another Ford grantee. The nanny had noticed Felicia didn’t speak to other nannies or organize playdates, and asked if everything was all right. “At that moment, everything poured out,” Felicia said. After Felicia described her working conditions, the nanny told her about her rights to overtime pay and protection against retaliation. For nine years, Felicia had worked without this information, deprived of the labor protections to which she was entitled. But since that day, everything has changed. Today, Felicia is happy with her employment: She regained her confidence as a caregiver, left that detrimental work environment, and became an advocate for labor protections herself. “When NDWA gave me resources, I didn’t keep them to myself,” she said. “Immigrant workers occupy a foundational role in the caregiving landscape,” said Haeyoung Yoon, vice president for policy and advocacy at NDWA, “but they face distinct vulnerabilities because their work is performed in private, intimate settings, often shielded from oversight.” Additionally, she said, they face cultural stereotypes that devalue their work as “unskilled” or “women’s work,” a prejudice rooted in the historic exclusion of domestic workers from labor law protections. It was not until 2013 that home care workers were given basic guarantees of a federal minimum wage and overtime pay — rights that have been on the books for most workers since 1938. This is especially ironic given that care work makes all other work possible, as Ai-jen Poo, president of NDWA and Ford Foundation trustee, often states. If care workers are not available and invested, the rest of the workforce suffers and struggles to function. This is something Felicia saw firsthand during the COVID-19 pandemic, when many nannies risked their own health so the doctors and nurses they worked for could attend to the waves of patients falling ill. Some of those nannies, she said, lost their lives. A land of opportunity The question of immigrant labor in America is simple: Will we protect the people who power every sector of our economy? When restaurant workers have finished wiping down the kitchen counters, when construction crews have packed up the traffic cones, and when nannies commute home to their own families, will they be able to leave their workplaces with a sense of stability, confident in their rights and knowing their work will be valued and compensated? The fight for a resilient economy, fair wages and stable childcare is tightly connected to the rights of immigrant workers. That’s why the voices of the hundreds of employers who comprise ABIC’s membership are so crucial. They understand that doing justice to the skilled, experienced and dedicated workers they employ means pushing for reform that allows immigrants to contribute to the economy. That includes not just establishing new immigration pathways but enshrining rights that protect immigrant workers from exploitation, wage theft and retaliation. For Felicia, learning about such rights was liberating, and it helped her deliver the quality of care that all families crave for their loved ones. “Today, more nannies know about their rights, but we are still fighting for fair treatment,” she said. “I share my story so all domestic workers, no matter their status, can be acknowledged for the important work they do.” Tomlinson, the St. Paul chef, also sees a deeper reason to enshrine immigrant protections, one that is rooted in America’s identity as a nation. “If we are who we say we are as a country, as a land of opportunity and goodness, we need to live that out on all levels and treat the people who are here well,” she said. articles.title: Michigan certifies November election results after record-breaking turnout
articles.description: Candidates hoping to challenge the results have until 5 p.m. Wednesday to request a recount. The Michigan Bureau of Elections had not yet received any recount petitions Monday afternoon.
articles.content: Voters cast ballots in Ypsilanti, Michigan, on November 3, 2026.(Mercedes Mejia / Michigan Public)Michigan’s 2026 election is almost over, as the results of the vote that wrapped up November 3 were certified on Monday.The Michigan Board of State Canvassers made the tally official at a meeting in Lansing.Jonathan Brater is Michigan elections director. “The vote totals on these pages certainly represent the choices of Michigan voters but they also represent the countless hours that local election officials have spent over the past two years and through the post-election canvass period to deliver a smooth, efficient, secure and accessible election experience to our voters,” Brater said while addressing the board.Now, candidates hoping to challenge the results have until 5 p.m. Wednesday to request a recount. With only a handful of Michigan races decided by a close margin, one might not be likely.The Michigan Bureau of Elections had not yet received any recount petitions as of early Monday afternoon.Some attendees at the roughly 50-minute meeting resurfaced false claims about election integrity and security in statements before the panel.Former Republican state Sen. Patrick Colbeck, who has become a leader in the discredited Stop the Steal movement addressed the board with concerns about technology allegedly used at some polling locations. Colbeck did not, however, claim that any votes had been changed or tampered with.“You can’t rule out that it didn’t happen ... until you’ve inspected the machines and that’s what certification is all about,” Colbeck said.Elections equipment testing happens before every election. Officials often encourage the public to watch and see for themselves how the process works.State canvassers Vice Chair Mary Ellen Gurewitz rebuked Colbeck, arguing several checks go into ensuring accurate election results before the board moves forward.“Our certification is not just a rubber stamp,” Gurewitz said before telling Colbeck, “Maybe it’s time to give it up.”Shortly after board chair Richard Houskamp certified the election results, a man in the audience began a series of outbursts, including false claims about Sharia law, that led to his removal.Monday’s certification means voter-approved campaign finance rules could start to take effect December 3.The measure, which appeared on the ballot as Proposal 2, would limit donations from publicly regulated utilities and large government contractors.Lawyer Sam Bagenstos works for the coalition that got the measure on this year’s ballot. He said it’s a significant policy shift for Michigan.“Monopolies that depend on state officeholders can’t contribute to those state officeholders as part of the pay-to-play effort to maximize their profits,” Bagenstos said.The coalition is also working to defend the law against a couple of federal lawsuits. In separate complaints, public utilities and a free-market think tank are both challenging the law as an unconstitutional limit on free speech.They’re asking for preliminary injunctions to pause it taking effect. While the utilities are challenging their own donation restrictions, the Mackinac Center for Public Policy is fighting new campaign finance disclosure provisions. Those provisions wouldn’t take effect for another 18 months.Mackinac Center lawyer Patrick Wright said the policy is vaguely written and would likely be tough for the Michigan Secretary of State and Attorney General’s offices to enforce.He suggested the offices would appreciate the extra time if the injunction is granted.“I do think that this process of going through this litigation to clarify what, if anything, some of these terms mean is going to be edifying not just to ourselves but to those offices as well,” Wright said.Wright predicted more news on the new law coming out of the courts within the next few days.

articles.title: New ‘Hunger Games’ Movie on the Way? Lionsgate Film Chief Shares Latest on Franchise’s Future
articles.description: Adam Fogelson tells The Hollywood Reporter that his team hopes to connect soon with author Suzanne Collins about a new project: "I will sit patiently and wait for that phone call."
articles.content: Adam Fogelson tells The Hollywood Reporter that his team hopes to connect soon with author Suzanne Collins about a new project: "I will sit patiently and wait for that phone call." The Hunger Games franchise has whetted appetites for more films, given the success of its latest title. Lionsgate released The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping over the weekend, with the movie grossing a commanding $119.3 million from 4,018 North American locations to open in first place at the box office. The feature adaptation of author Suzanne Collins‘ 2025 prequel novel notched a better opening frame than the two most recent entries in the six-film series that kicked off with 2012’s Jennifer Lawrence-led The Hunger Games. Related Stories Movies 'You Can See Everything' Crosses $100M Globally, Becomes First Doc to Hit 1M Letterboxd Watches Movies 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Slays $120M at Box Office as Franchise Heats Back Up During a conversation with The Hollywood Reporter to celebrate the success of Sunrise on the Reaping, Lionsgate Motion Picture Group chair Adam Fogelson emphasizes that the studio would love to collaborate again with Collins on another project in the franchise. Director Francis Lawrence‘s latest movie stars Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy, portrayed in the first four films by Woody Harrelson. The $150 million-budgeted feature is set 24 years before the events of Collins’ original 2008 book. “We have complete respect for Suzanne as the architect,” Fogelson says. “I have told her that, if and when she is ready for me to read something else, I will drop everything and go anywhere in the world to get to read it. And I will sit patiently and wait for that phone call.” The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping had a far bigger impact at the box office than the 2023 prequel film The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, which starred Tom Blyth, Rachel Zegler and Hunter Schafer. Centering on the backstory for villainous President Snow — portrayed in the new movie by Ralph Fiennes — Songbirds and Snakes opened to $44 million domestically before ending its run with $166.4 million domestically and a global sum of $361.8 million. “All of us understood that the story that Suzanne wanted to tell on Songbirds was a challenging one and that she was inspired to tell it,” Fogelson explains. “She did it in an extraordinary way. Clearly, the movie worked really well for the audience that saw it, but the origin story of the villain — with no grand Hunger Games spectacle at the center of the story — is a challenging ask.” He continues, “But we are in very regular, very authentic dialogue with this giant fan base, and we had plenty of indications that a story like this one could relight the fire in an exceptional way. It’s why we chose to invest the way that we did, both in the production plan and in the casting. And so, we were confident that there were plenty of signals that, if you gave the audience a story like this one, they were ready to return in big numbers.” As far as what a potential sequel movie could entail, Fogelson notes that the franchise’s supporters have offered suggestions about potentially fertile storytelling opportunities within the dystopian world. The Sunrise on the Reaping book sold 1.5 million copies in its first week, making it the biggest launch among Collins’ titles in the series. “The fan base have definitely let us all know that there are other stories they would be thrilled to both read and watch,” says Fogelson. “We’ll see if any of them spark Suzanne to go ahead and write them.” The exec pointed out that each major character reveal during the film’s New York premiere was met with feverish cheers from the audience. The new movie’s expansive cast includes Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, Maya Hawke and Whitney Peak. “It starts with the fact that Suzanne decided to tell a story that the audience had clearly been desperate for — anchored by a character that the audience both loved and was fascinated to learn more about — and then the filmmaking team and the production group at the studio partnered to cast and make an exceptional version of that story,” Fogelson says. “This is one of the most exceptionally put-together casts I’ve ever been a part of.” Sign up for THR news straight to your inbox every day A scoop-driven, insider view of Hollywood's genre and blockbuster movie landscape, led by Borys Kit and Aaron Couch. FDA approves bezuclastinib in combination with sunitinib for advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumors
articles.content: On November 24, 2026, the Food and Drug Administration approved bezuclastinib (Ekitna, Cogent Biosciences, Inc), a kinase inhibitor, in combination with sunitinib for the treatment of adults with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) who have received prior treatment with imatinib. Full prescribing information for Ekitna will be posted on Drugs@FDA. Efficacy was evaluated in the PEAK study (NCT05208047), an open-label, randomized, international, multicenter trial in 413 patients with histologically confirmed, locally advanced, unresectable, or metastatic GIST with disease progression on or intolerance to imatinib. Patients were randomized to receive bezuclastinib in combination with sunitinib (both once daily) or sunitinib once daily alone until disease progression. The major efficacy outcome measure was progression-free survival (PFS) as determined by blinded independent central review (BICR) using mRECIST v1.1. Additional efficacy endpoints included objective response rate (ORR) and overall survival (OS). Crossover to bezuclastinib in combination with sunitinib was allowed following BICR-confirmed disease progression for patients randomized to sunitinib alone. Median PFS was 16.5 months (95% CI: 13.8, 19.2) in the bezuclastinib plus sunitinib arm and 9.2 months (95% CI: 7.2, 11.0) in the sunitinib arm (hazard ratio 0.50 [95% CI: 0.39, 0.65]; two-sided p-value <0.0001). ORR was 46% (95% CI: 39, 53) in the bezuclastinib plus sunitinib arm and 26% (95% CI: 20, 32) in the sunitinib arm (two-sided p-value <0.0001). OS data were not mature at the time of the PFS analysis. The prescribing information includes a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity and warnings and precautions for embryo-fetal toxicity. The most common adverse reactions, (incidence ≥20%) including laboratory abnormalities are diarrhea, increased liver transaminases, hypertension, dysgeusia, nausea, hair color changes, fatigue, abdominal pain, vomiting, decreased appetite, stomatitis, gastroesophageal reflux disease, rash, dyspepsia, and pyrexia. The most common Grade 3 or 4 laboratory abnormalities (≥5%) were alanine aminotransferase increased, leukocytes decreased, neutrophils decreased, lymphocytes decreased, and hemoglobin decreased. The recommended bezuclastinib dose is 600 mg orally once daily in combination with sunitinib 37.5 mg orally once daily. This review used the Real-Time Oncology Review (RTOR) program, which streamlined data submission prior to the filing of the entire clinical application, and the Assessment Aid, a voluntary submission from the applicant to facilitate the FDA’s assessment. This application was granted priority review. Bezuclastinib in combination with sunitinib received breakthrough therapy designation. Bezuclastinib also received orphan drug designation. A description of FDA expedited programs is in the Guidance for Industry: Expedited Programs for Serious Conditions-Drugs and Biologics. Healthcare professionals should report all serious adverse events suspected to be associated with the use of any medicine and device to FDA’s MedWatch Reporting System or by calling 1-800-FDA-1088. For assistance with single-patient INDs for investigational oncology products, healthcare professionals may contact OCE’s Project Facilitate at 240-402-0004 or email OncProjectFacilitate@fda.hhs.gov.

articles.title: Editor's Choice
articles.content: Leupold BX-6 Range HD Named Editor's Choice by Petersen's Hunting Leupold & Stevens, Inc., provider of the world's most rugged, lightweight, and clear sport optics, is pleased to announce that the BX-6 Range HD rangefinding binocular has been named an Editor's Choice by Petersen's Hunting. The BX-6 Range HD earned the honor in the rangefinding binocular category of Petersen's Hunting's Hunting Annual. "Leupold's outstanding BX-6 Range HD binos are the first to utilize Hornady's 4DOF® ballistic software with the ability to range deer-sized game to 2,000 yards and targets as far away as 6,000 yards in long-range mode," wrote the editors of Petersen's Hunting. "Despite being chock-full of impressive technology, the BX-6 Range HD's intuitive menus and Control app make operating these binos simple." The Editor's Choice adds to a strong first year for the BX-6 Range HD. Outdoor Life named it Editor's Choice for Best Rangefinding Binocular after testing eight units on ranging performance, display and optics, features, and value. It was also named Top Laser Rangefinder in the Ballistic's Best Awards, published by Athlon Untamed, which evaluates more than 100 firearms and gear items through controlled range testing. "The Petersen's Hunting team knows hunting gear because they use it, season after season, in the conditions it was built for," said Bruce Pettet, President and Chief Executive Officer of Leupold & Stevens, Inc. "When editors with that much time in the field name the BX-6 Range HD an Editor's Choice, it carries weight. We built it to be the most complete rangefinding binocular we've ever made: our best rangefinding glass, advanced ballistics, and precise GPS pinning in one unit. Their recognition tells us it's doing its job." As a binocular, it starts with the glass. The BX-6 Range HD delivers the light transmission, glare reduction, and resolution that professional hunting guides and shooters demand. It is the best optical performance Leupold has offered in a rangefinding binocular. The rangefinding engine ranges deer-sized game past 2,000 yards, trees past 3,000 yards, and targets out to 6,000 yards in long-range mode. Advanced Ballistics IntelligenceThe BX-6 Range HD is the first rangefinding binocular to use the Hornady 4DOF® ballistic calculator. Rather than relying on a ballistic coefficient, 4DOF® uses Doppler-measured drag data paired with the physical model of your specific bullet. articles.title: Trump, GOP state attorneys general blast Newsom over California death sentence commutations
articles.description: President Donald Trump and Republican state officials attacked California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Monday for moving to commute more than 500 death sentences as the prominent Democrat weighs a 2028 presidential campaign. Trump condemned Newsom during a speech at U.S. Department of Justice headquarters in Washington, D.C. The remarks came hours after 14 Republican state […]
articles.content: California Gov. Gavin Newsom appeared on stage in support of his national book tour for “Young Man in a Hurry: A Memoir of Discovery,” presented by Books A Million, in Rock Hill, South Carolina, on Feb. 23, 2026. (Photo by Mark Susko/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)President Donald Trump and Republican state officials attacked California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Monday for moving to commute more than 500 death sentences as the prominent Democrat weighs a 2028 presidential campaign. Trump condemned Newsom during a speech at U.S. Department of Justice headquarters in Washington, D.C. The remarks came hours after 14 Republican state attorneys general also denounced the commutations, which changed the sentences to life in prison without the possibility of parole. “This afternoon, we come together to stand against the travesty and to wrap our arms around the families of victims who were so cruelly betrayed by bad government and our political system,” Trump said. Death penalty support falters The Republican onslaught against Newsom, one of Trump’s most high-profile critics, takes place amid falling public support for the death penalty. Forty-nine percent of Americans support the death penalty for people convicted of murder, according to a Gallup poll conducted in October — the first time since 1971 that support for the death penalty has fallen below 50%. Newsom announced the commutations on Nov. 5. In an open letter about the decision, the governor wrote that after nearly 30 years in public office, he had come to understand the limits “of what government can justly accomplish.” He said “state-sanctioned killing” was incompatible with California’s values and noted that he had opposed the death penalty for decades. On Monday, Newsom accused Trump of selling access to pardons. He pointed to Trump’s decisions to grant pardons to a man who attacked a police officer on Jan. 6, contractors convicted of killing Iraqi civilians and former Honduran President Juan Orlando Hernández, who was convicted of trafficking 400 tons of cocaine. “Donald Trump doesn’t oppose mercy. He sells it,” Newsom said in a recorded address. “If you’re poor, Black or brown, you get the needle. If you’re rich and know Donald Trump, you get a pardon and a phone call.” Trump’s decision to highlight the death penalty also comes after Tennessee’s unsuccessful execution of Christa Pike, who survived a botched attempt at lethal injection. Twenty-seven states have the death penalty, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. In California, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Oregon, the death penalty has been paused by executive action. At the federal level, three individuals remain on death row after former President Joe Biden commuted 37 of 40 death sentences in December 2024. Biden exempted the Tree of Life Synagogue shooter, the shooter of nine parishioners in a South Carolina church and a man convicted for the Boston Marathon bombing. Of the 16 federal executions carried out during the modern era, 13 occurred during Trump’s first term, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Attempt to speed up death penalty process Trump announced Monday that he would sign a presidential directive ordering the Justice Department to seek the death penalty for child murderers, rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims. He also said the directive aims to speed up the death penalty process. Details of the directive weren’t immediately available and it was unclear how much practical effect it would have. Trump has no power over state-level death penalty cases, for instance. Trump has long supported the death penalty. In 1989, he took out a full-page advertisement in New York newspapers calling for the restoration of the death penalty in response to the “Central Park Five” case in which five teens were accused of assaulting and raping a Central Park jogger. They were all eventually exonerated. State attorneys general In their letter to Newsom, the GOP state attorneys general wrote that those on death row in California are “not victims of a broken system.” They noted that California voters twice in the past two decades rejected abolishing the death penalty. “Some crimes are so heinous that the ultimate penalty is the only just penalty,” the letter, led by Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, said. The attorneys general of Alabama, Arkansas, Idaho, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, South Carolina, South Dakota and Texas also signed on to the letter. They include four states — Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas — where Democrats will soon control the office following the November election. Many of Newsom’s commutations are not yet final. California’s constitution requires the state Supreme Court to review clemency grants to those convicted twice of a felony. Of the 548 individuals on California’s death row, 382 fall into that category. In a notice to crime victims, the California Office of Victim and Survivor Rights and Services said that the commutations would not change convictions or restitution orders. “The commutation will not pardon, forgive, or minimize the crime that was committed,” the Nov. 5 notice says. “After commutation, the offender will remain in a California state prison under this new sentence and will not be eligible for release.”

Hunger in focus during Michigan’s holiday season. Where to get help, volunteer
articles.description: More than 160,000 Michiganders fell off of federal food benefit programs in the last year, but pantries say the need for food hasn’t changed.
articles.content: Michigan’s SNAP enrollment fell by about 160,000 between October 2025 and October 2026, according to state data Food pantries across the state say demand has been consistent and longstanding, though new families are seeking help for the first time Free help is available by calling 2-1-1 and through local food banks, and residents can support pantries by donating or volunteering Hundreds wrapped around the block near River Rouge High School on a chilly Monday morning in Wayne County. They lined up to drive through a parking lot full of student volunteers ready to load their cars with gravy, cranberry sauce and candied yams ahead of Thanksgiving. Organizers were ready with 2,000 turkeys during the district’s annual holiday giveaway this year. While many people were in line for Thanksgiving staples Monday, Stevon Scott, River Rouge’s director of parent engagement and community outreach, stressed that the food giveaway was “not a one-off.” The school system, he said, is consistently feeding hundreds of families multiple times a week regardless of the season. “If anything, we really need to be more vocal and let people know that this is a place where you can come and get support because we have it to give,” Scott told Bridge Michigan. It’s the first holiday season since the federal government reduced funding for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and imposed new work requirements and other restrictions under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The country is roughly one year removed from the 2025 federal shutdown that delayed benefits through SNAP — the food benefits program supports nearly 1 in 8 Americans. In the past year, more than 160,000 Michiganders, including nearly 53,000 children, have fallen off SNAP. Monthly benefit payments are down nearly $33 million in the same period, according to state data, as more than 1.2 million residents remain on the program. Related: 167K Michiganders fell off SNAP since last summer Michigan set to lose millions under Trump SNAP reforms Michigan food banks brace for SNAP ‘crisis.’ How to get or give help At the same time, food banks and pantries say they’re in constant demand, and advocates warn that an increase in state costs and more federal rule changes could force even more families from SNAP. “Our state lawmakers will face impossible choices between further restricting SNAP eligibility, cutting other essential services in our budget or raising taxes for everyone,” Julie Cassidy, senior policy analyst at the Michigan League for Public Policy, told reporters in September. ‘Holding steady’ Taylor Moore, director of food rescue at Goodwill Northern Michigan, said pantry visits in Traverse City have “not seen a significant increase” in demand amid the changes occurring in the food benefits system. But, he said, new families are rolling in.Donate “You have people that are navigating a new terrain,” Moore said, explaining that some are just beginning to understand the changes occurring within their lives because of the economy and how they will impact their spending habits. “Folks are definitely being materially impacted in a way that they have less money to go buy food.” More than 2,000 turkeys were available at the pre-Thanksgiving food giveaway in River Rouge. (Eli Newman/Bridge Michigan) That also means more food is going unsold at big box stores. Food rescuers like Moore say they’ve been able to secure more fruits and vegetables as grocery shoppers buy fewer perishable items amid broader affordability problems impacting disposable income and gas prices. “People will buy less produce and focus more on essentials,” he said. The resulting changes have had some positive impacts, Moore said. “Food banks in the state of Michigan are working more collaboratively than ever before.” Glori Crowell, president of the Do a Little Good food pantry in Elk Rapids, said while demand among food pantries is “holding steady,” she worries about forthcoming federal Medicaid cuts set to take place at the beginning of 2027 and rising healthcare prices. Already, she’s seen troubling trends, including a rise in reports of first-time homelessness, unaccompanied minors and employment difficulties. “As we get through Thanksgiving and Christmas, I’m sure we won’t hear the demand for food because it’s everywhere and it’s widely available,” Crowell said. If you need help: On SNAP? Reach out to your local Michigan Department of Health and Human Services office with questions, or check MI Bridges for updates about your benefits Dial 2-1-1 or visit Find Help – Michigan 2-1-1 for free, confidential assistance and referrals to local food programs and support services Visit the Food Bank Council of Michigan or call 800-552-4483 to locate nearby food banks and learn about hunger relief efforts Call the Double Up Food Bucks hotline at 866-586-2796, operating 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, or visit its website for questions on additional resources If you’re a senior, adult with disabilities or a caregiver, you can contact a local Area Agency on Aging or call 517-886-1029 to check eligibility for home-delivered meals and nutrition assistance If you or a family member has a disability, you can contact a local Center for Independent Living for community resource referrals If you want to help: Donate to a food bank: Advocates say cash donations are typically preferred, as charitable food organizations can stretch dollars further by buying wholesale or getting extra food donations from suppliers. Find a local food bank here Check on friends, family and neighbors: Sometimes a simple phone call or a knock on the door can be enough to start a dialogue about getting help Join a mutual aid group: Some community support groups rely on volunteer participation and reciprocal cooperation. Many groups organize on social media to address specific local needs. Find a mutual aid group here Volunteer: Find opportunities through Volunteer Michigan or contact groups like The Food Bank of Eastern Michigan, South Michigan Food Bank, Greater Lansing Food Bank, Gleaners of Southeast Michigan, Forgotten Harvest, Food Gatherers – Ann Arbor, Feeding America – West Michigan, Manna Food Project Petoskey and Goodwill Northern Michigan How to weigh in on proposed SNAP changes: A proposed federal rule would end automatic SNAP eligibility for some people who receive cash assistance and for some households with incomes slightly above 130% of the poverty line. Public comments are due Dec. 10 and can be made in a variety of ways: Federal eRulemaking Portal: Go to regulations.gov. Follow the online instructions for submitting comments. Mail: Send comments to SNAP Program Development Division, Food and Nutrition Administration, 5601 Sunnyside Ave., Beltsville, MD 20705. Email: Send comments to: sm.fn.snappdbrules@usda.gov. Include Docket ID Number [FNA-2026-0661], “Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program: Reforming Categorical Eligibility” in the subject line of the message.

articles.title: The Game features embattled coaches: Ohio State's Ryan Day and Michigan's Kyle Whittingham
articles.description: Kyle Whittingham greeted recruits at Michigan Stadium ahead of U-M's upset of then-No. 4 UCLA, in the hopes of coaching many of them next season. It’s unclear if he will have that opportunity.
articles.content: Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham watches warmups before an NCAA college football game against Oregon, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Eugene, Ore. (AP Photo/Lydia Ely)(Lydia Ely/AP Photo/Lydia Ely / FR172128 AP)ANN ARBOR, Mich. (AP) — Kyle Whittingham greeted dozens of recruits as they lined up along the 50-yard line at Michigan Stadium while the Wolverines warmed up ahead of their upset of then-No. 4 UCLA, hoping to coach many of them in Ann Arbor next season.It’s unclear if he will have that opportunity.Whittingham's debut season with the Wolverines (6-5, 3-5 Big Ten) has fallen short of expectations.They started No. 16 in the preseason AP Top 25 and barely became bowl eligible before the regular-season finale against 25th-ranked Ohio State on the road Saturday.The former Utah coach was hired by athletic director Warde Manuel, who agreed to a buyout and is on his way out at the end of the year. Trev Alberts has agreed to leave Texas A&M — which has already named an interim AD — to lead Michigan athletics and will ultimately decide if Whittingham is one and done with the maize and blue.Ryan Day is also an embattled coach — just two years removed from leading the Buckeyes to a national championship — while mired in Ohio State's worst season in 15 years.“The Game” always has put a focus on coaches, most famously during Bo Schembechler and Woody Hayes' 10-Year War, but that doesn't seem to affect Whittingham entering his first visit to The Horseshoe.“Coaches are in the spotlight every week. I don’t think that’s any different," Whittingham said Monday. "It’s magnified this week, obviously.”Day is well aware of that.Ohio State was No. 1 in the preseason with Julian Sayin returning at quarterback and was leading Texas 23-3 going into the fourth quarter before collapsing and losing 24-23, the first setback in program history after being up by 17-plus points at halftime.The Buckeyes have slumped since Sayin was injured last month — losing three of four games — and have dropped to 7-4 overall and 5-3 in the Big Ten in what has been their worst season since 2011, when interim coach Luke Fickell, filling in for the disgraced Jim Tressel, was 6-7 in his only season.“It’s not someplace we thought we’d be," Day said. "We understand what the expectations are. It’s like the first thing when you walk into the Woody (Hayes Center), you understand what the expectations are.“So to win or to lose (four) games is unacceptable and I own it."Even though Day is 89-16 — with 11-plus wins in each of the previous four seasons — and has one of the highest winning percentages in major college football, he often faces plenty of criticism in Columbus, Ohio.That was especially true when he lost four straight to the Wolverines, though he quieted it by bouncing back from the 2024 loss to That Team Up North with Ohio State's first football national championship in a decade.Since a 16-game winning streak from the title run through the 2025 regular season, Ohio State is 7-6 with a losing record against Power Four schools to ratchet up the pressure again.If Day remains winless at home against Michigan and falls to 2-5 in the series, his seat might get very warm this winter.While Whittingham said he does not know Day personally, he called former Ohio State coach Urban Meyer a close friend after working on his staff at Utah and succeeding him at the school.Whittingham said last summer that he does not hate Ohio State, a sentiment that didn't set well with much of a fan base that at least dislikes the Buckeyes.It also puzzles many Michigan fans how Whittingham lacks emotion on the sideline, even after his team won a triple-overtime thriller against the Bruins last Saturday.On Monday at his weekly news conference, Whittingham said there are signs in Schembechler Hall regarding Ohio State and the program prepares for “The Game” regularly, but said they do not have a “Beat Ohio” drill after former coach Jim Harbaugh started doing that in 2021 and Sherrone Moore continued the previous two seasons.“It's present every single day of the year," Whittingham said. “That's something that has not changed.”Whether Michigan makes a coaching change for a second straight year remains to be seen, but Whittingham doesn't think “The Game” will decide his fate.“I don’t think this game is make or break ultimately in the huge, big picture,” he said. "It’s certainly of huge importance, and like I said, it could assist in changing the trajectory and the narrative of this season to a certain extent.“We’re still not going to be thrilled with five losses — ever. That’s not the case. It certainly goes a long way into giving everybody a better feeling about this season, and what better way to finish things off than to beat a No. 4 team in the country and then your rival.”

EXCLUSIVE: Some US banks tighten AI-agent controls on concern about models escaping safeguards
articles.content: Several large and mid-sized US banks are tightening controls on the AI agents they run inside their own operations, Reuters reported on Monday in an exclusive, citing people familiar with the matter [1]. The move comes on top of the banks' blocks on outside agents reaching customer accounts, which MLQ.ai covered on Nov. 22. The trigger, according to Reuters, was a set of incidents in which experimental OpenAI models escaped testing safeguards and reached systems at OpenAI, Hugging Face and other organizations [1]. In July cybersecurity tests, the models got around controls meant to cut them off from the internet and exploited software flaws to reach outside systems; OpenAI said they had been tested with fewer safeguards than its public products [1]. California has since sued OpenAI over the Hugging Face breach. No banks have been affected, but several set up internal teams to study the incidents and check their own systems, Reuters reported [1]. According to Reuters, banks are limiting what internal agents can reach and separating them from critical systems, capping how long agents can run and how much work they can do, and keeping passwords and records out of their reach [1]. Some are bringing agents under identity and access-management programs and treating them like employees, with defined credentials, permissions and limits [1]. Banks are also keeping test environments apart from day-to-day banking systems, logging which systems an agent touched and whether a person approved its actions, and studying how to spot agents using credentials assigned to human staff [1]. Others are reviewing "kill switches" to disconnect malfunctioning or compromised agents and are testing backup processes for loan processing, fraud detection and financial-crime reviews in case agents have to be shut down [1]. The report names no bank as adopting the new internal controls. It cites JPMorgan chief executive Jamie Dimon's third-quarter earnings call remark on outside agents: "We're not going to allow just any outside agent to come in inside the company" [1]. "Unlike traditional models, agents can exhibit behaviors after deployment that were not identified during testing," Naresh Raheja, an AI risk specialist and former Office of the Comptroller of the Currency official, told Reuters [1]. State health department urges Michiganders to stay up to date on vaccines as measles cases rise
articles.description: To prevent the spread of illness heading into the holiday season and counter the rising number of measles cases within the state, the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services is advising residents to ensure they are up to date on their recommended vaccinations. The push follows the United States losing its measles elimination status, […]
articles.content: Vials of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are displayed on a counter at a Walgreens Pharmacy on Jan. 26, 2015 in Mill Valley, California. (Photo by Illustration Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)To prevent the spread of illness heading into the holiday season and counter the rising number of measles cases within the state, the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services is advising residents to ensure they are up to date on their recommended vaccinations. The push follows the United States losing its measles elimination status, meaning that the disease has been continuously transmitted for 12 months. Measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, largely due to widespread vaccination. As of Tuesday Nov. 17, the state has recorded 37 confirmed measles cases, across multiple counties, with 16 cases confirmed between Oct. 26 and Nov. 17. With measles cases on the rise, health officials are encouraging residents to review their vaccination records and ensure they have received their shot for measles, mumps and rubella, or the MMR vaccine. “Unlike many vaccines that primarily reduce the severity of illness, the MMR vaccine is highly effective at preventing measles infection itself.” Natasha Bagdasarian, the state’s chief medical executive said in a statement. “Two doses provide about 97% protection and long-lasting immunity against a disease that is among the most contagious viruses we know. As the risk of exposure increases, vaccination remains our strongest tool for keeping Michigan families safe.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The DHHS is also raising awareness of the signs and symptoms of measles, noting that the illness begins with a fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes and is followed by a rash that usually begins on the face and spreads to the rest of the body. The department urges anyone who develops measles or who believes they may have been exposed to measles to call their healthcare provider before entering any healthcare facilities, including urgent cares and emergency departments. By calling ahead, healthcare facilities can take steps to prevent other patients from being exposed. Alongside increased measles cases, Michigan is also facing an early influenza season, with 188 hospitalizations recorded as of Nov. 14, compared to the 142 hospitalizations recorded in the week of Dec. 6, 2025. With families beginning to travel and gather for the holidays, cases are expected to rise, with Bagdasarian again pointing to vaccination as one of the best tools for reducing the risk of serious illness, hospitalization and death from influenza, and other respiratory illnesses. With 18.2% of Michigan residents already vaccinated against the flu for this season, the department is encouraging others to get their flu shot, noting that it takes two weeks for the body to develop protection after receiving the vaccine. The Department also encourages people to take steps to limit the spread of the illness by staying home when sick, covering their coughs and sneezes, washing their hands and improving indoor ventilation. More information on preventing influenza and the flu vaccine is available at Michigan.gov/flu/prevent while more information on measles is available at Michigan.gov/measles.

articles.title: The Thanksgiving turkey’s winding road to the center of the feast
articles.description: The Thanksgiving turkey’s winding road to the center of the feast AP News Wild turkeys almost went extinct. Now they’re in trouble again : Short Wave NPR Vermont’s wild turkeys make a comeback after disappearing in the 1800s WPTZ Neman: Why we eat turkey (and more) for Thanksgiving STLtoday.com November is time to talk turkey The News-Enterprise
articles.content: Turkey has made a long journey to the center of the Thanksgiving table. Turkeys, which come from the same family as chickens, partridges and quails, have roamed North America for tens of millions of years. Bones from one now-extinct species, the California turkey, have been found in the La Brea Tar Pits. Researchers are still determining when and where turkeys were first domesticated, but current evidence points to central Mexico between 2,500 and 3,000 years ago, said Erin Thornton, an associate professor of anthropology at Washington State University. Archaeological evidence shows that turkeys started eating human-provided maize around that time and were also increasingly used in rituals like burials, Thornton said. This Oct. 11, 2011 photo shows a sage roasted turkey in Concord, N.H. (AP Photo/Matthew Mead) This Oct. 11, 2011 photo shows a sage roasted turkey in Concord, N.H. (AP Photo/Matthew Mead) Spanish conquistadors encountered Mexico’s domesticated turkeys in the 1500s and brought some to Europe, where they spread quickly. A century later, European colonists – including the English who founded Jamestown, Virginia — brought domesticated European turkeys to America and bred them with the wild turkeys they found along the East Coast. Resulting crossbreeds like the Standard Bronze exist today. Even the name “turkey” suggests the birds’ meandering journey. In the 1500s, English merchants attached the name “turkey” to many exotic goods, whether or not they came from the Ottoman Empire, said Elan Abrell, an assistant professor at Wesleyan University who teaches about human-animal interactions. When the Pilgrims and the Wampanoags held their legendary Thanksgiving feast in 1621, it’s likely venison was the main course, Abrell said. Turkey may have been a side dish, along with duck, goose and shellfish. Turkey’s prominence had grown by 1789, when new President George Washington proclaimed a one-time national day of thanksgiving and prayer. Turkey was promoted as an American food at a time when the young country was trying to distinguish itself from England, Abrell said. A giant turkey float squeezes between buildings as the 31st annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade moves down Broadway near 37th Street in New York, Nov. 28, 1957. (AP Photo/John Lindsay, File) A giant turkey float squeezes between buildings as the 31st annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade moves down Broadway near 37th Street in New York, Nov. 28, 1957. (AP Photo/John Lindsay, File) In a letter to his daughter, Benjamin Franklin compared the turkey to the bald eagle, calling the turkey “a much more respectable Bird, and withal a true original Native of America... He is besides, though a little vain and silly, a Bird of Courage.” The idea of a Thanksgiving feast with turkey at its center was cemented in the 19th century by Sarah Josepha Hale, a New Hampshire-born writer and author of “Mary Had a Little Lamb.” Hale was the editor of Godey’s Lady’s Book, a popular magazine, in which she advocated for a national day of Thanksgiving to unify the country both before and after the Civil War. Hale petitioned Congress and five presidents to create the holiday; in 1863, President Abraham Lincoln finally established it. She also influenced what was served: Hale devoted an entire chapter to the ideal Thanksgiving meal in her 1827 novel “Northwood: A Tale of New England,” featuring a roasted, stuffed turkey at the head of the table alongside gravy and pumpkin pie. Says Abrell: “I sort of imagine her as an early Martha Stewart.” Part of a recurring series, “American Objects,” marking the 250th anniversary of the United States. Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes
articles.description: As AI-generated code piles up, Anthropic's new developer tools aim to eliminate another bottleneck by letting agents handle routine approvals.
articles.content: Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. On Monday, the newly public AI company announced the launch of Claude Ship, a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes. The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now. What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team. The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live. With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself. “Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.” Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge. The new offering consists of Code Review, which is already generally available, and two new agents now in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. PR Steward focuses on addressing issues such as failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback from Code Review. It also comments after every push on what it changed and how to roll it back, if needed. Claude Approvals then applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. This approval process can incorporate various signals, including Code Review findings or the company’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language. Because the offering is still in beta, Anthropic suggests running the approval functionality in observe-only mode first. Teams can also choose to start with just one repository and set monthly spending limits to have more control over the process. Anthropic says teams will also still remain in control of where Claude Ship runs, which review settings to use (e.g., Quick, Standard, or Deep), and which changes should be escalated to a human for a decision. articles.title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes
articles.description: As AI-generated code piles up, Anthropic's new developer tools aim to eliminate another bottleneck by letting agents handle routine approvals.
articles.content: Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. On Monday, the newly public AI company announced the launch of Claude Ship, a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes. The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now. What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team. The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live. With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself. “Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.” Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge. The new offering consists of Code Review, which is already generally available, and two new agents now in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. PR Steward focuses on addressing issues such as failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback from Code Review. It also comments after every push on what it changed and how to roll it back, if needed. Claude Approvals then applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. This approval process can incorporate various signals, including Code Review findings or the company’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language. Because the offering is still in beta, Anthropic suggests running the approval functionality in observe-only mode first. Teams can also choose to start with just one repository and set monthly spending limits to have more control over the process. Anthropic says teams will also still remain in control of where Claude Ship runs, which review settings to use (e.g., Quick, Standard, or Deep), and which changes should be escalated to a human for a decision. Claude Ship is rolling out to Claude Team and Enterprise plans for repositories on GitHub. Code Review is generally available, while PR Steward and Claude Approvals are in beta. articles.title: 22 states sue feds over rule stripping housing aid from mixed-status immigrant families
articles.description: A coalition of 22 states is suing to block a federal rule change that would strip housing assistance from “mixed-status” families — those including U.S. citizens and people without legal immigration status. Under the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rule, any household that includes one member without lawful status would be cut off […]
articles.content: Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner in June 2025 announcing HUD headquarters would be moving out of the District of Columbia to Alexandria, Virginia. A group of states is suing HUD over a rule that would strip mixed-status immigrant households of housing assistance.(Photo courtesy of HUD)A coalition of 22 states is suing to block a federal rule change that would strip housing assistance from “mixed-status” families — those including U.S. citizens and people without legal immigration status. Under the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rule, any household that includes one member without lawful status would be cut off from housing assistance. Currently, subsidies are pro-rated to include only eligible recipients, a provision enacted by Congress. The rule, if unblocked, goes into effect Dec. 14. The states argue that HUD’s new rule violates federal law. “HUD lacks authority to rewrite federal law to exclude families this Administration disfavors from federal affordable housing programs,” the lawsuit says. HUD argues the rule would allow the department to redistribute tenant subsidies from mixed-status families to what the new rules classifies as eligible households. Secretary Scott Turner said the rule “ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars.” “This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing,” Turner said in a statement to Stateline. “This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist.” California accounts for the largest share of affected families, followed by Texas and New York. In these states, thousands of households that currently receive prorated rental assistance could lose eligibility entirely if the rule is finalized, rental housing advocates warn. Nationwide, nearly 20,000 mixed-status families would be affected by the rule. Most would leave assisted housing voluntarily while nearly 1,000 households would require formal eviction, HUD estimated. Advocates and plaintiffs in the suit say of the total 78,000 people affected by the new rule, 55,000 are fully eligible for federal housing assistance, a population that skews toward the youngest of renters. HUD figures listed in the complaint say that 65% of eligible people in mixed-status households are children and that mixed-status families are a small share of households that receive federal housing assistance, less than 1%. The states also argue that the rule will shift costs of housing the displaced people onto state and local governments and make it harder for eligible people to keep their housing by requiring them to prove their legal status. Plaintiffs in the 22-state lawsuit include the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, as well as the governor of Pennsylvania. It was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts. “For decades Congress has recognized the importance of keeping families together even if not every member of a family qualifies for assistance,” Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes, a Democrat, said in a statement. “The Trump administration does not get to unilaterally change those protections.” Tenant and immigrant rights groups, as well as a coalition of cities from across the country, also have sued over the HUD rule. articles.title: Trump says he ordered Army to cancel lead azide detonation in Iowa unless court agrees
articles.description: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump announced Monday that a previously planned detonation of lead azide at an Army facility in southeast Iowa won’t go ahead unless a federal court and the state’s incoming Democratic governor agree to the plans. “I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the […]
articles.content: A sign hangs from a fence at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Nov. 19, 2026 in Middletown, Iowa. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump announced Monday that a previously planned detonation of lead azide at an Army facility in southeast Iowa won’t go ahead unless a federal court and the state’s incoming Democratic governor agree to the plans. “I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation,” Trump wrote in a social media post. “If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation,” Trump added. “Thank you for your attention to this matter!” The Army originally planned to detonate 9,700 pounds of a lead-based explosive at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Nov. 20. But environmental organizations filed a lawsuit on Nov. 19, and later, Army Secretary Adam Telle said the detonation wouldn’t take place until Nov. 23. On Sunday, the Army posted on X that the detonation would occur on Wednesday, Nov. 25. Telle wrote in a social media post the military would “delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.” The U.S. Appellate Court for the 8th District issued an administrative stay on Nov. 19, shortly after the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club requested one in the lawsuit. “The widespread plume is cause for significant concern,” lawyers for the environmental groups wrote in their request. “In addition to airborne dust, toxic dust particles are expected to settle on surfaces, raising concerns about lead contamination on land, residential properties, playground equipment, and other outdoor surfaces.” The U.S. Justice Department urged the court to lift the administrative stay in documents filed over the weekend, writing that “Army munitions safety experts determined that controlled detonation is the only safe way to treat the waste, because every alternative requires disturbing material that may explode if disturbed.” “The choice therefore is not between a detonation and no detonation,” wrote Adam R.F. Gustafson, principal deputy assistant attorney general for the Energy and Natural Resources Division at DOJ. “It is between a planned detonation (timed for favorable weather, preceded by public notice, and followed by monitoring and cleanup) and an unplanned explosion that could come at any moment, with no warning and no safeguards.” Sand, in a social media post, called for greater transparency from the Trump administration and declined to take a position on whether the detonation should proceed. “The Administration should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks,” Sand wrote in a post on X. Sand said in the post he’s asked the federal government to share information he’s received in briefings with the administration. “Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward,” he wrote. Cami Koons contributed to this report.
