articles.title: Megaspeed, the company at the center of the Jensen Huang scandal, appears headed for a US blacklist
articles.description: Megaspeed, which was previously led by Alice Huang, would be barred from doing business with U.S. companies unless those companies attained a special license from the federal government.
articles.content: Megaspeed, the company that Alice Huang — the woman at the center of the alleged Chinese espionage scandal involving Nvidia — led for over two years, will be placed on a U.S. Commerce Department blacklist, Semafor reported Monday. The company will be added to the Commerce Department’s Entity List, the outlet writes. This list “contains the names of foreign parties” subject to certain export restrictions designed to ensure that “sensitive technologies do not fall into the hands of those who would threaten U.S. national security or American citizens.” Functionally, what this will mean is that U.S. companies will not be able to do business with or sell products to Megaspeed without first gaining a special license from the federal government. Semafor cites anonymous sources familiar with the matter to note the move is designed to stop the company “from obtaining US-made semiconductors.” Megaspeed is a Singapore-based cloud and AI infrastructure provider that, during the period that Nvidia’s boss, Jensen Huang, self-admittedly had an affair with Huang, was one of Nvidia’s biggest chip customers. Last week, the Commerce Department also announced it had launched a criminal probe into the company. Authorities in both the U.S. and Singapore are now probing whether the company defied export restrictions and illegally smuggled Nvidia chips to China. The company has denied wrongdoing. TechCrunch reached out to the Commerce Department for comment on the reporting and will update this story if it responds. After lobbying from President Trump, Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia CEO on Monday after a short period in which he was ousted by the company’s board over the scandal involving Huang. articles.title: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
articles.description: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo, an open-source runtime for Linux. It helps teams protect running systems while they roll out patches.
articles.content: An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test(opens in a new window), a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart. We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day. Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline. Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running. Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems. How the guardian agent observes and protects a running system with eBPF. OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities: Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it. Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed. Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes. Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements. The Shirudo technical walkthrough(opens in a new window) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to apply a shield and verify it on the target host(opens in a new window). The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more here(opens in a new window). Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer. Our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to quickly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. Applications should run with only the permissions they need, governed by policies that are automatically generated and maintained. We will combine frontier AI with security and infrastructure research to discover vulnerabilities and test defenses against realistic attacks. We aim to make it easier for operators to detect and contain compromises, prevent attackers from moving across systems, and restore services to a verified, known-good state. Hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls provide additional assurance even if individual systems are compromised. OpenAI and Cisco are open-sourcing Shirudo(opens in a new window) so developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators can inspect the code, test protections, and contribute to its development. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL. Our goal is to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches. Try Shirudo: Follow the VM quickstart(opens in a new window) to sign, load, and verify a test protection. Get hands-on: Explore Shirudo through Isovalent's self-guided lab(opens in a new window). Join the technical deep dive: Register for the December 15 webinar(opens in a new window). We’re building Shirudo in the open with the people who build, run, and secure Linux systems. We welcome contributions to the runtime, new shields, and improvements to Linux and eBPF. If you'd like to get involved, take a look at the code on GitHub(opens in a new window), read the docs(opens in a new window), and let us know what you find(opens in a new window).

articles.title: Gary Peters reflects on US Senate career, criticizes Pete Hegseth on Iran
articles.description: Retiring Michigan Sen. Gary Peters talks with Stateside about the 2026 Senate race, advice for the incoming Democratic majority and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
articles.content: FILE - Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., speaks during the Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Pete Hegseth, President-elect Donald Trump's choice to be Defense secretary, at the Capitol in Washington, Jan. 14, 2025. (AP Photo/Ben Curtis, File)(Ben Curtis/AP / AP)U.S. Sen. Gary Peters (D-Michigan) is retiring from office after two terms in the U.S. Senate and 18 years in Congress. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed will succeed him after defeating Republican Mike Rogers in the 2026 midterm election.Stateside Host April Baer sat down for an interview with Peters reflecting on his time in office, advice for the incoming batch of Senators, and whether he thinks there are stewards in place to take care of our service members.The following is a snippet from the conversation. You can listen to the full conversation above.April Baer: How do you feel about the campaign that we’ve just all been through to select your replacement?Gary Peters: It was a pretty intense campaign and, unfortunately, it was incredibly nasty. I mean, the Republicans, I think, really took the campaign to a new low. The personal attacks on Abdul were outrageous and certainly unacceptable, and surely I think it was a sign of their desperation. But I'm tired of seeing that in American politics.It does not strengthen our democratic process certainly. And I would hope at some point, particularly after it was unsuccessful, that that may change things in the future, but I'm not naive about that either. We’re probably likely to continue to see it.AB: The new majority — including Senator-Elect Abdul El-Sayed, who will be stepping in to your shoes — have made no bones about the fact that they want to make progress quickly on things that they promised during the campaign: ending the war in Iran; doing things about the cost of living; and starting to address the health care crisis.A think tank at Vanderbilt called you the No. 1 most effective member of the U.S. Senate. What advice would you have for the new majority on moving forward quickly?GP: First off, it is about, kind of, building relationships and working together. You know, the advice I give to every new member that comes into the Senate is, I say, 'Remember the campaigns over. And now you have the privilege of representing everybody in your state, not just those that voted for you.'You're not gonna obviously change who you are, your core beliefs. I’m a proud Democrat and I've always been a proud Democrat and will continue to be such, but there are a lot of things that we can figure out together and try to take some of the hyperpartisanship out in order just to solve things.Ideally, that's what I would certainly like to see, but you know we do have an advantage as Democrats right now is that we have very large majorities. So, you can take some pretty bold action. And you should.Certainly the election I think was very clear by voters all across the country. And especially these red states that we really thought we could be competitive, but not win as much as we did. I mean, to think that Texas now is a blue state. People are basically giving Democrats a shot, a chance to show what we can do and it's important for us to take some pretty, pretty bold action.But, while you're doing that, obviously trying to build consensus in the Senate. So you need to figure out how do you do that in a way that builds the broad consensus and also gives more permanence. You want to be able to move policies forward that also have staying power. We just don't swing back and forth in elections. That's not healthy for the constitutional democracy that we have, so trying to find that common ground while being bold at the same time is really important.AB: Senator Peters, you're a service member yourself, retired, and a lot of your terms have been spent making sure that military members, active duty, and veterans have been cared for. I'm also thinking a lot about the situation that this country finds itself in now with its military and its just a fractious time as there are many, many Americans who have concerns about what's going on in Iran and the U.S. military has been under more and more pressure because of changing federal mandates. I wonder, as you're getting ready to exit the Senate, if you think the stewards are there to take care of our service members in the way that they deserve.GP: Well, certainly, I have real problems with Secretary (Pete) Hegseth. I think he's operating way over his head. He is the wrong person for that job. I'd say he’s probably the least qualified individual we've ever had as Secretary of Defense. We're paying the price for that. His personnel actions can't be defended. We're certainly seeing that, which is having an impact on morale with our troops. And, the fact that he pushed so aggressively for this action in Iran has been disastrous.But I'm very concerned about leadership, to your point, and this, the action in Iran and launching those attacks before our military was really ready to do things like make sure the Strait of Hormuz wasn't shut down, really shows a failure of leadership.You know, I called out Secretary Hegseth pretty aggressively in a hearing not too long ago, that this is not a failure of the men and women who serve every day, who put their lives on the line and serve with honor and distinction. This was a failure of political leadership over the military. And that goes right to him and to President Trump and folks in the administration and they need to be held accountable for that.This transcript has been edited for length and clarity.

articles.description: Retired detective is jailed in road rage killing on a bridge in New York City AP News Retired Detective Scrubbed Car After Road-Rage Shooting, Prosecutors Say The New York Times GWB road rage: Victor Romero ordered held without bail in George Washington Bridge shooting ABC7 New York He tried to merge on the George Washington Bridge. A minute later, he was fatally shot. CNN Bail revoked for ex-cop accused of shooting
articles.content: NEW YORK (AP) — A judge revoked a long-retired New York City police detective’s $1 million bail Monday in a road rage killing on the George Washington Bridge, sending the former officer to jail to await trial in what’s now a murder case. After initially facing a manslaughter charge, Victor Romero pleaded not guilty Monday to a murder indictment in the Oct. 20 death of Koran Irvine. A message seeking comment was sent to Romero’s attorney. Romero, 62, and Irvine, 46, got into a near-collision on an on-ramp to the bridge, prosecutors said. They said Romero then tailed Irvine’s car, pulled up near it — in Irvine’s blind spot — and shot him through his back passenger window as both motorists headed toward New Jersey. Irvine, an electrical utility employee on his way home from work, was shot in the torso, with the bullet piercing his heart and both lungs. Romero drove off, authorities said. Prosecutors initially charged Romero with the lesser offense of manslaughter, and he was released on $1 million bail last month. But a grand jury then indicted him on a murder charge, at prosecutors’ suggestion. Manhattan Assistant District Attorney Matt Sears said in court Monday that prosecutors now have more evidence, including video of Romero wiping down the driver’s side of his car and the driver’s seat area on the morning after the shooting, while not cleaning the rest of the vehicle. When police approached him later that day and asked about the car, he told them he “didn’t get into an accident,” according to a court filing from prosecutors. A semiautomatic pistol found in his home matched a bullet from Irvine’s body and a shell casing discovered in Romero’s own car, Sears said. He asked for Romero to be held without bail. Romero spent six years with the New York Police Department before retiring in 2001. He had been wounded in an off-duty shootout with men attempting to rob his family’s laundromat. Irvine’s family had publicly pushed for a murder charge, and the relatives and their lawyer said the outcome of Monday’s arraignment was a step toward justice. “But it’s not going to bring him back,” sister Zeria Irvine said, choking up, to journalists outside the courthouse.

articles.content: Anthropic is launching some new Claude AI features to help software engineers ship code. As part of a new Claude Ship product being announced today, Claude now can review, fix, and approve pull requests. Engineers have already been able to take advantage of Claude’s code review capabilities thanks to the Code Review feature, which was announced in March and became generally available in October. What’s new alongside Claude Ship are the PR Steward and Claude Approvals agents, which are launching in beta today. PR Steward “jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members” and leaves comments on what it changed, according to Anthropic. Claude Approvals can approve routine changes if an organization’s policy allows it. “Teams can have Claude Approvals consider a variety of signals in its decision-making process, including Code Review findings or their own classifiers using natural language,” Anthropic says. Claude Ship is now available for Claude Team and Enterprise customers and works with repositories on GitHub.

articles.title: East Lansing Considers Local Control of Saginaw Street, Grand River Avenue
articles.description: If the city takes control of the major roads, it could amend speed limits. However, it would also have to pay for repairs.
articles.content: Multiple crashes involving pedestrians, including an incident in which an 86-year-old was struck by a cement truck, have prompted the East Lansing Transportation Commission to consider whether the city should take over management and maintenance of two major roads that bisect the community. At its Nov. 2 meeting, the Transportation Commission invited representatives from Kalamazoo, Meridian Township and Ann Arbor to share their experiences working with the Michigan Department of Transportation. Each municipality has successfully taken control of a road previously managed by the state. The two roads under consideration in East Lansing are Saginaw Street and Grand River Avenue. Commission member Noah Vander Galien, who invited the representatives to the meeting, said three or four crashes involving pedestrians occurred near the intersection of Saginaw Street and Abbot Road over a six-week period. Those incidents, combined with frequent requests from community members urging the commission to take action, have prompted discussions about whether the city should assume control of the roads. If the city does take control of the roads, it would be able to adjust the speed limits and change the signal timings at some intersections. However, the city would also need to pay for road repairs. “I think that that’s the biggest sticking point as far as the city’s concerned; that’s a big expense that right now we don’t have to pay,” Vander Galien said. Currently, Vander Galien said, the city can contact the Michigan Department of Transportation, or MDOT, when a state-managed road needs repairs. Speaking for himself and not on behalf of the commission, Vander Galien said he believes a truly vibrant downtown is difficult to achieve without changes to Grand River Avenue. “We’re getting close to the age where there’s driverless cars, and people have electric cars, and everything else, and the problems are only getting worse,” he said. “There are only more delivery drivers downtown, there are only more deliver-like big trucks that just block a lane on Grand River that in order to have a truly like vibrant economic center of the town, I think that something needs to change about how traffic moves through it.” Vander Galien said the presentations from Kalamazoo and Ann Arbor demonstrated how flexible MDOT can be when working with municipalities. Erin Chelotti, manager of MDOT’s Lansing Transportation Service Center, helped coordinate a transfer of state-managed roads with the city of Lansing. She spoke with East Lansing Info about how such agreements work. Chelotti explained that the state and municipality start with a conversation about if the transfer makes sense. If discussions advance, entities would then develop a memorandum of understanding identifying the condition the road should be in before ownership is transferred. In Lansing’s case, the city and state exchanged responsibility for different roads. The state received Michigan Avenue from East Lansing to the freeway, while Lansing took control of a portion of the Capitol Loop previously managed by MDOT. The exchange took nearly two years, Chelotti said, because both parties had to agree on the condition of the roads before the transfer could be completed. “In that situation,” she said, “we actually both gained continuity in our networks versus losing continuity, so it really made a lot of sense for us to make that transfer. It helped both of us out.” Vander Galien emphasized that the Transportation Commission is not yet ready to recommend that the city take over either road. However, he expects discussions to continue. “I think that it’s important to encourage people to come to Transportation Commission meetings or City Council meetings and express their opinions about the matter,” he said. articles.title: Reports: Russia may launch nuclear weapon into orbit as soon as next month
articles.description: A nuclear detonation in space "could cause rapid and sudden loss or degradation of thousands of satellites."
articles.content: Western intelligence officials worry that Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite into orbit before the end of the year, suggesting the country's development of a satellite-killing weapon of mass destruction is more advanced than previously thought, German media reported Monday. The orbiting nuclear weapon would threaten thousands of satellites in low-Earth orbit, including military and commercial communications networks like Starshield and Starlink. A nuclear-armed satellite would also put at risk Western military surveillance satellites and human spaceflight platforms like the International Space Station. A nuclear detonation in orbit would be indiscriminate, also knocking out Russia's own spacecraft and Chinese satellites. US lawmakers briefed on government intelligence first disclosed Russia's ambition to deploy a space-based nuclear weapon in early 2024. At the time, US officials said Russia had launched a test satellite in 2022 to test the effects of radiation on space hardware and pave the way for a future nuclear-armed craft, but that Russia had not yet sent a nuclear weapon into orbit.Read full article Comments

Coffia, Grand Traverse Democrats urge Benson to remove utility-linked members from transition team
articles.description: The presence of three members on Democratic Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson’s transition team — who are closely associated with the state’s regulated utilities — has raised concerns from some Democrats over the impact they could have on Benson politically when she takes office in January. Over the weekend, the Grand Traverse Democratic Party and one of […]
articles.content: Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson spoke to reporters the morning after winning the gubernatorial election, telling reporters that her agenda for the first 100 days would be rolled out soon. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)The presence of three members on Democratic Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson’s transition team — who are closely associated with the state’s regulated utilities — has raised concerns from some Democrats over the impact they could have on Benson politically when she takes office in January. Over the weekend, the Grand Traverse Democratic Party and one of its leaders, state Rep. Betsy Coffia (D-Traverse City), both called on Benson to immediately remove Gary Torgow, Fadwa Hammoud and Mel Brown from her transition team. The party noted that Torgow sits on DTE Energy’s corporate board, and that Hammoud and Brown both work for Miller Johnson, the law firm that represents both DTE and Consumers Energy. Miller Johnson is currently engaged in a federal lawsuit, representing the utilities, in a bid to stop Proposal 2 of 2026, known as the Michiganders for Money out of Politics, from taking effect. The ballot proposal passed by a wide margin on Nov. 3. It seeks to prevent DTE and Consumers Energy from using corporate money to make political contributions and to prevent the utilities, or any other large corporation that holds contracts with the state, from influencing politics in Michigan. In a statement to Michigan Advance, Benson transition team spokesperson Amber McCann said that “bringing people together to drive down costs, grow our economy and achieve bold change is key part of Governor-Elect Benson’s approach to transforming Michigan. “She will work with anyone to make that happen, and looks forward to continuing to bring together diverse leaders from across the state who are willing to partner with her to achieve those ambitious goals,” McCann said, who also noted that the transition leadership council will conclude its work next week Monday. “The Governor-Elect looks forward to continuing to engage leaders in every community to advance her bold and ambitious agenda to drive down costs, increase wages, and end corruption,” McCann added. McCann did not directly acknowledge the calls to remove Torgow, Hammoud and Brown to be taken off the team. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Hammoud also previously worked with the Department of Attorney General under Attorney General Dana Nessel, as she was one of two special prosecutors tasked with investigating the Flint Water Crisis. Still, the Grand Traverse Democratic Party said Benson’s decision to place them on the transition team was disappointing, and that removing them would help Benson avoid corporate influence on her decisions as governor — especially as it concerns Proposal 2. “Michigan voters passed that proposal with 81 percent of the vote,” the party wrote in a statement issued Sunday. “Michigan voted to take money out of politics, not to give it to a seat on a transition team. It was our honor to have you launch your campaign for governor in Grand Traverse County, and we are asking you to stay committed to the will of Michigan voters.” At its most recent convention, the Grand Traverse Democrats said, it passed a resolution to send Benson a letter calling on Torgow, Hammoud and Brown to be taken off the team. Their members also urged Benson to support bills to regulate corporate spending power in Michigan elections currently allowed by the Citizens United court precedent, as well as the Bringing Reforms in Integrity, Transparency and Ethics or BRITE Act, which would improve government accountability standards. “Voters delivered an overwhelming mandate, and we need action,” the Grand Traverse Democrats wrote in a letter to Benson. “We stand ready to help you deliver it.” Rep. Betsy Coffia (D-Traverse City) speaks at a news conference in Lansing to unveil government transparency legislation on March 13, 2024. (Photo: Anna Liz Nichols) Coffia sponsored the House version of the Citizens United bills, and she similarly called for Benson to remove Torgow, Hammoud and Brown. “I have a lot of respect for Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson and believe there is much good we can accomplish in the coming legislative term. That is why I must state publicly, with all due respect to the Governor-elect, it is inappropriate and a clear conflict of interest to put DTE board members and lawyers connected to the lawsuit to block MMOP on the Governor elect’s transition team,” Coffia said in a Facebook post. “This is especially glaring given the brazen bad faith actions by the utilities trying to stop the will of over 80% of Michigan voters who just weeks ago overwhelmingly approved the MMOP ballot initiative to stop the utilities and government contractors from giving political donations. Michiganders have spoken. They don’t want big money players steering Michigan’s politics any longer.” Coffia continued by saying that Michigan’s government needs to be receptive to its constituents and set a clear foundation for Benson’s earliest days as governor. “All transition team members with ties to the utilities, government contractors and the lawsuit against MMOP need to be removed from this important PUBLIC INTEREST role,” Coffia wrote. “The people of Michigan have high expectations of us and a great need for their leaders to bring our A Game. Let’s give it to them.” 3:42 pmThis story was updated to include a comment from Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson's transition team.

FDA Approves First Treatment for Limb-Girdle Muscular Dystrophy Type 2I/R9
articles.description: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved the first medicine for treating limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2I/R9 (LGMD2I/R9), a rare inherited muscle disease, for adults and pediatric patients weighing at least 30 kg.
articles.content: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Welgemda (ribitol), the first medicine for treating limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2I/R9 (LGMD2I/R9), a rare inherited muscle disease, for adults and pediatric patients weighing at least 30 kg. Welgemda is the first therapy approved for any form of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy. “Today’s approval is a historic milestone for patients and families living with limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, delivering the first-ever FDA-approved treatment for this disease, backed by clinical evidence,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “Under the Trump Administration’s commitment to accelerating innovation and removing unnecessary barriers for rare disease therapies, while maintaining high standards for safety, the FDA is proud to deliver real hope and meaningful progress for patients who have waited far too long for options.” LGMD2I/R9 is caused by mutations in the FKRP gene, which disrupt a key biological process in muscle cells. In healthy individuals, the FKRP enzyme helps attach sugar molecules to a protein called alpha-dystroglycan, which acts as an anchor, helping muscle cells connect to surrounding tissue. When this process is disrupted, muscle cells become fragile and break down over time, leading to progressive weakness, difficulty walking, and in many patients, impaired breathing. Symptoms typically appear in childhood or early adulthood and worsen over time. “Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy is a progressive muscle disease that gradually takes away a patient’s ability to walk, breathe, and live independently, often beginning in childhood,” said Laura Jawidzik, M.D., Director of the Division of Neurology 2 in the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. “The clinical data supporting Welgemda's approval show meaningful improvements in walking speed and lung function, and we are encouraged by what that can mean for patients' daily lives.” The precise mechanism of Welgemda in the treatment of LGMD2I/R9 is not fully known, but may involve increases in a natural sugar molecule (matriglycan) that anchors alpha-dystroglycan in muscle tissue. The medicine is taken as an oral solution twice daily, mixed with water. Welgemda was evaluated in a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study (NCT05775848) involving 112 patients with genetically confirmed LGMD2I/R9. Patients were randomly assigned to receive either Welgemda or placebo for up to 36 months. At a planned interim analysis after 12 months of treatment, patients receiving Welgemda showed significant improvements in two key measures compared to those receiving placebo. Specifically, patients showed improvements in walking speed, measured by the 100-meter timed test, and lung function, measured by forced vital capacity (an indicator of respiratory muscle health). Patients treated with Welgemda also showed significant increases in glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan, indicating the drug was reaching its intended target at the proposed dose. The most common adverse reactions were gastrointestinal effects (e.g., diarrhea, stomach pain) and joint pain. Welgemda received Orphan Drug, Fast Track, and rare pediatric disease designations for the treatment of LGMD2I/R9. Welgemda is manufactured by ML Bio Solutions Inc. and distributed by BridgeBio Pharma, Inc. articles.source: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content: Mamdani said he will have surgery on Friday to address his torn Achilles tendon. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he will undergo surgery later this week for a soccer injury he sustained during a friendly match with the press last week. "I'm scared; it will be my first surgery," Mamdani said during an unrelated news conference on Monday. Mamdani said his surgery is scheduled for Friday morning. "I'll be down from about 9 a.m. to 2 p.m.," he said. "I'll be laid out for a couple of days." While he is in surgery, First Deputy Mayor Dean Fuleihan will be mayor, Mamdani said, adding, "we will be following the legal order of operations." The mayor previously told reporters that he tore his Achilles tendon during a soccer match against the City Hall press corps on Thursday. He has since shown up to public events on crutches, with a boot on his right foot. Mamdani said he "did not stretch" before taking to the pitch, and that he tore the tendon soon after scoring a goal. articles.content: See It Stick it, Sight Words (ages 3-7, $21.99) from Mrs. Wordsmith accelerates a child’s reading with colorful and fun stickers for every word. Our second-grade toy testers loved the stickers and how it uses a QR code to read the words. They said they would like to see something similar for math. Five stars! Kids Book Projector (3-up, $75 ) from Luna Storytime was a big hit with our toy testers. Landyn, 18-months, listened to the read-aloud stories with his brother, Jack, 8, both of whom enjoyed their time together, especially seeing the story projected on the wall. Another 2-year-old tester also enjoyed seeing the stories come to life. Their parents’ only problem was the volume was too loud. Wooden Little Doc’s Medical Kit (3-up, $29.99 ) from Jasey’s Toy Chest was a big hit with all of our preschool testers. They loved pretending to be doctors and taking care of each other. In fact they had so much fun they would like to see the elves make a big, colorful pretend hospital with beds, doctor tools, an ambulance and even a little X-ray machine to go with it. Five stars! Moosh-Moosh Holiday Collection (3-99, $14.99) from K2A Brands is a cool group of squishy toys for children and even adults. Our fourth-grade testers, Juliana and Alaya, said there’s nothing to dislike about these fluffy and soft toys. Characters in the collection are inspired by Christmas-themes including Jack, Yuki, Mitzy, Eduard and Mintie. Peppa Pig Ready, Pedal Go (3-up, $39.99) from Hasbro had all of our preschool toy testers wanting to give it a try. They loved making Peppa ride her bike. She fell off a couple of times and they found that frustrating, so Santa’s elves need to improve on that, but overall the toy was a big hit. They enjoyed the bright colors, fun sounds and watching Peppa pedal. Five stars! Off to the Rescue Vehicle Carrier (3-up,$24.99) is another award-winning toy made by Jasey’s Toy Chest. Our preschool toy testers loved driving the little cars up and down the ramp, pretending they were delivering them to different places. They especially loved seeing how many cars they could fit on the carrier, which comes with four wooden emergency vehicles. One tip for the elves: add something to keep the cars in place. Five stars! Oppenheim Toy Portfolio Gold Seal Award Winner! Bluey Cruise Ship Playset (3-up, $59.99) from Moose Toys comes with 5 play pieces and five play areas. Our preschool toy testers had great fun playing with the slide and pretending Bluey was sailing across the ocean on a cruise vacation. Five stars! Drop (3-up, $8.99 ), as in gooey, stretchy gum drop is one of several in a line of squishy toys from Master Toys. Others from this company include: Holiday Qubes ($7.99) and squishy food such as Slow Rise Pancakes, Sprinkle Donut, Macaroons ($10.99) or Squishy Trend Dill Pickle (3-up, $4.99 ). Our preschoolers loved playing with the soft and squishy. pancakes and butter. Their teacher said they had fun squeezing the food and watching it slowly return to their originalshape. They couldn’t stop touching them. Five stars! Wooden Busy Wheels Garage Playset (3-up, $84.99 ) from Jasey’s Toy Chest was a big hit with our toy testing tykes. Their preschool teachers said the children absolutely loved watching the little cars race down the ramps and pretending that they were parking their cars and going on little adventures. The elevator was a big hit too. Tips for the elves: Make the elevator a little easier for smaller hands and add a few more cars so everyone can join in the fun. Mighty Morphin Power Rangers: Re-Ignition Ultimate Megazord Electronic Figure (3-up, $29.97) by Playmates Toys. Our toy testers CJ and Roman loved the cool weapons and the noises it made but said its hands need to be bigger in order to hold the swords. Clickblocks Kinetic Puzzle (3-10, $15) from Watchitude is a cool new toy that kids can use to build six different puzzles. Designs include: Dinosaurs, Sweet Treats, Flying Machines and Unicorns. Rowan, 9, liked how the pieces click together to form a cube and that one puzzle can become another, and another. Fourth-graders, Scarlett and Max, loved that it was both challenging and fun. Older kids might also enjoy the bigger 27-piece Clickblocks puzzle. Five stars!

Amazon snaps up Decart’s AI optimization tech for $7.5B as it prepares to sell Trainium chips
articles.description: Amazon is acquiring Decart’s AI optimization technology and research team in a reported $7.5 billion deal.
articles.content: Amazon has agreed to acquire a good chunk of Israeli startup Decart. The e-commerce and cloud giant is paying $7.5 billion for the startup, according to Bloomberg. Decart has made a name for itself building interactive real-time world models — most recently Oasis 3 — and AI video-generation tools. But under the hood, the company stands out for its Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), software that helps AI models run efficiently on Nvidia, Amazon, and Google’s hardware. As part of the deal, Amazon will acquire the technology behind DOS, as well as Decart’s founding team and team of AI researchers and engineers, Amazon said in a blog post. “Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, quantum computing, at Amazon. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost.” Amazon, which has so far been using its Trainium chips at its own data centers, is preparing to start selling them to customers as a competitor to Nvidia. Decart’s technology could make it easier for customers to run their workloads on Amazon chips, rather than Nvidia’s, which has been the gold standard so far. Decart and Amazon did not immediately return requests for comment. Michigan has spent $40M trying to fix foster care. Abuse is increasing
articles.description: For 18 years, a federal court has overseen Michigan’s system of caring for the state’s 9,200 foster children. Audits continue to cite flaws, but Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s administration wants to end a consent decree.
articles.content: The rate of abuse and neglect of foster care children in Michigan is on the rise despite 18 years of federal oversight Michigan is now seeking to end that oversight, arguing it is ‘archaic’ and no longer helping to improve the system But federal monitors say the rising abuse and neglect rates are an ‘urgent safety threat to children’ LANSING — After 18 years and at least $40 million spent on the court-monitored overhaul of Michigan’s child welfare system, abuse and neglect are on the rise in state foster care. That “represents an urgent safety threat to children,” federal court monitors wrote in a recent report, the latest development in the long-running saga. The warning came as the Whitmer administration seeks to end the oversight, arguing the more than $2 million a year it is spending on those federal monitors would “be far better spent on children and families in Michigan.” The work to reform Michigan’s child welfare system began two decades ago, with a 2006 class action lawsuit claiming the system “inflicts numerous harms” on the children it is responsible for protecting. Those reported harms included maltreatment and neglect for children in foster care, a lack of “basic” healthcare, excessive lengths of stay in the system and frequent changes in their primary caregivers once the state got involved. Rather than defend itself, the state settled the suit in 2008, agreeing to give federal monitors extensive authority to oversee mandated improvements. Related: Michigan wants out of child welfare oversight. Other states offer road map Michigan foster kids struggle under system that gives ‘nothing’ after aging out Where former foster youth in Michigan can get postsecondary aid, training Michigan under pressure to end ‘orphan tax’ on benefits for foster youth Two administrations and several state health directors later, Michigan has failed to meet 19 of 24 performance measures and is “moving in the wrong direction” when it comes to preventing abuse and neglect of children in state care, federal monitors wrote in their July report. About 9,200 children were in state care last year, and the monitors cited 447 substantiated abuse or neglect incidents in their July report — 163 more than the minimum standard. They also reviewed a random sample of 150 state abuse and neglect investigations and found that a third “were not undertaken adequately.” Under the current agreement, Michigan is judged by the rate of child victimizations for every 100,000 days in foster care. That rate topped 14 last year, up from 5.6 in 2021 and higher than the 9.07 federal benchmark.Donate Those findings were revealed one month after Michigan urged a federal judge to end the long-running monitoring. Despite struggles to meet the federal benchmarks, most Michigan children in foster care are safe, according to an expert the state hired as part of the case. Though “initially beneficial,” the consent decree governing the foster care program “has become archaic” and is “premised in outdated theories of child welfare,” Assistant Attorney General Neil Giovanatti wrote in a June filing. It now “imposes unnecessary and harmful burdens on both the state and children in foster care.” In a June court filing, Michigan asked a federal judge to end long-running oversight of its child welfare system even though it had not met most benchmarks for improvement. (Asha Lewis / Bridge Michigan) Samantha Bartosz, an attorney for Children’s Rights, the group that filed the 2006 lawsuit, opposed the state’s request, arguing in a court filing that “(d)ifficulty or inconvenience” in meeting required metrics does “not legally justify the modification of a consent decree.” The state’s request to end the federal oversight should “absolutely not” be granted, said state Sen. Jim Runestad, who organized a foster care reform rally at the Michigan Capitol last spring. “The state of Michigan never takes this seriously,” he said. “There’s always failures in every single audit report I’ve seen. Colossal failures.” Runestad, a White Lake Republican who also chairs the state Republican Party, said public safety should be the number one priority for governments, and protecting children is the “number one of the number one.” “And they fail at that,” Runestad said of the state. “And they never, ever will put forth the resources to fix the problem.” ‘Where’s the boat oar you beat your kids with?’ A recent Clinton County trial detailed the consequences that can fall on children when a system fails. Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel said Tamal and Jerry Flore “subjected their foster and adopted children to prolonged, routine and systemic mental and physical abuse all for personal financial gain” over the span of 14 years. When she first brought charges in 2023, Nessel said the allegations “highlight not only a moral and legal failure of those entrusted with the children’s care, but a failure in our systems to ensure children placed in custody are properly taken care of.” The couple took in some foster children, who were later adopted. At trial, testimony from police, medical experts and adopted children described beatings with a 35-inch boat oar, meals withheld, bedrooms that could only lock from the outside, security cameras in the children’s bedrooms and children being forced to live in a laundry room as punishment. Authorities said the abuse began in 2009, but the criminal investigation leading to charges started in 2021 when Clinton County Sheriff Sean Dush, who was a detective at the time, accompanied a CPS investigator to the Flore home to execute a search warrant as part of a child abuse investigation. “I walked in the house and I went to Jerry and I asked, ‘Jerry, where’s the boat oar you beat your kids with?’” Dush testified. “… He walked right upstairs without saying a word and pointed it out in the closet in the master bedroom.” From 2010 through September 2021, the Flores received about $1.7 million from the state in the form of adoption subsidy payments, according to testimony. In late October, Tamal Flore, 59, was convicted on 11 felonies, including five first-degree child abuse counts that carry maximum sentences of life in prison. Jerry Flore, 61, was convicted on a second-degree child abuse charge and faces up to 10 years in prison at sentencing, which is scheduled for January. Jerry Flore plans to appeal his conviction, his attorney told Bridge Michigan. Tamal Flore’s attorney declined to comment. The CPS investigator who was with Dush during the 2021 search of the Flore home was later suspended and then fired, she testified, for failing to follow protocol. She interviewed some children, who still lived in the home, inside a sheriff’s office patrol vehicle, contrary to forensic interview protocol. She had received a six-week training course on the protocol when hired less than two years prior. She also made errors in her notes from the interviews and attributed some comments to the wrong child when submitting her report. She testified that those errors and others were caused by limited time and resources. The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services runs the state’s child welfare system, which has been under federal oversight since 2008. (Robin Erb/Bridge Michigan) State says money for monitor better used for MDHHS staff Under the terms of the 2008 consent decree, Michigan is paying for the federal monitors who are tasked with overseeing improvements to the state’s child welfare system. Costs connected to the lawsuit and monitoring have exceeded $40 million, according to the state. In 2025 alone, the state spent about $2.7 million on monitors. But as it seeks to end the federal oversight, Michigan argues it could better serve children and families by using that money to hire an estimated 18 additional “CPS investigators, foster care case managers, or other staff.” Staff shortages were among the initial problems detailed in the 2006 litigation, and the consent decree set specific caseloads standards, which required the state to add staff. National standards at the time called for one caseworker for every 10 to 15 children in the system. But Michigan caseworkers were sometimes managing 25 to 40 children each, according to the 2006 lawsuit. Despite adding staff, the state struggled with high turnover rates and inexperience, said Sarah Font, who was hired as a Michigan child welfare worker in 2008 and is now a researcher at Washington University in St. Louis. During her 2 ½ years with the state, Font said she had three different supervisors, and after just six months on the job, she had new employees shadowing her. Most of her eight-week training was spent on learning the internal data system and applicable laws, and not much time on the investigative process, Font told Bridge. “Parents just don’t admit to whatever the allegations are,” she said. “You need really strong investigation and observational skills to know what’s going on.” The confrontational nature is present in well-run systems, she said, so CPS investigators have to be comfortable walking into someone’s home where they’re not wanted and facing hostility. Font said it’s not uncommon for reviews of child fatalities to show that an investigator was timid or had limited access to the child. “And that’s where, I think, really serious risks or safety issues get missed or unaddressed,” Font said. In January, the family of 5-year-old Ethan Belcher, who was killed by his mother and her boyfriend, sued the state in federal court. Ethan was killed less than two years after a CPS investigation was opened, and the lawsuit claims the state failed to properly investigate, the Detroit News reported. Child welfare systems are “probably the most difficult public service to operate,” said Jill Berrick, a University of California, Berkeley expert who added that a CPS investigator is trying to make the best estimate about a child’s safety under difficult circumstances. “It’s a system of scarcity,” she said. “There’s scarcity of time. There’s a scarcity of money. There’s a scarcity of great community members stepping forward to be a part of kids’ lives.” State: Most abuse, neglect happens in kinship homes Michigan’s rate of child victimization per day in foster care has exceeded the federal benchmark for abuse and neglect in each of the past three years. But in general, “children in foster care are safe” despite those metrics, Joseph Ryan, a University of Michigan professor, said in his expert report submitted as part of the state’s request to end the federal monitoring. While there were 447 substantiated instances of abuse and neglect in Michigan over the prior year, children were in the foster care system for a collective 3.1 million days. “This translates into one (instance) for approximately every 7,000 days of foster care,” Ryan wrote. The state had hired Ryan, director of U-M’s Child and Adolescent Data Lab, to provide an assessment of permanency outcomes, the use of emergency shelters and the incidents of abuse and neglect in state care. From 2021 to 2024, about 1% of foster care children in Michigan were abused or neglected, Ryan wrote. That is higher than the 0.6% national average and put Michigan among the 10 worst-performing states. But, he cautioned, comparing rates between states is “not advised” because they have different policies, reporting systems, investigatory practices and data quality. Ryan also found that “the largest share” of Michigan’s maltreatment in care incidents occurred in what’s known as kinship care, when a child is placed with relatives. As of 2024, more than half of Michigan foster children resided in kinship homes, according to his analysis, which found that unsupervised and unapproved visits with biological parents are frequent factors for these incidents. articles.title: Michigan wants out of child welfare oversight. Other states offer road map
articles.description: Michigan is asking a judge to end federal oversight of its child welfare system. But it hasn't met benchmarks, unlike two other states that successfully complied with similar requirements. Here's how they did it.
articles.content: Michigan is seeking end federal monitoring of its child welfare system despite failing to meet benchmarks Wisconsin and Connecticut successfully exited monitoring the past five years, ending oversight prompted by similar lawsuits Michigan said the consent decree and monitoring has cost it at least $40 million. The state argues the oversight is no longer helpful LANSING — Michigan officials are asking a federal judge to end the 18-year monitoring of the state’s child welfare system, arguing that initially helpful oversight is now “antiquated” and getting in the way of reforms. More than a decade before Michigan was sued over widespread foster care failures, similar litigation prompted federal oversight in Wisconsin and Connecticut, both of which successfully exited monitoring in the past five years. The three states were all sued by Children’s Rights, an advocacy law firm that focuses on exposing and combating violations of the rights of children. The organization has sued 26 states, leading to monitoring in at least nine, with more than a dozen active cases. Wisconsin successfully exited monitoring of its child welfare operations in Milwaukee in September 2021, when US District Court Judge Pamela Pepper described the conclusion as a “celebration” of the efforts by the state, child welfare staff, the plaintiffs and others who had often been in disagreement over nearly 19 years. US District Court Judge Pamela Pepper, seen here in 2014, on Capitol Hill in Washington, oversaw child welfare monitoring in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. (Harry Hamburg/Associated Press) By 2021, medical care, dental care and other services provided to children in the system had “improved substantially,” according to court records. The state remained short on one remaining performance measure: the percentage of children in the system who had three or fewer placements over a three-year period. The goal was 90%, and Wisconsin had been at 87% or higher for at least seven years. There was acknowledgment in court filings and during a hearing that no system is perfect. “It’s one of the few moments in my career, they don’t happen a lot, where I find myself in the presence of a group of people who at one point were not at all united in their view of the system, but now are,” Pepper told attorneys, public officials and advocates gathered in her Milwaukee courtroom. “And all of whom have worked, in their own way and in their own capacity, to better the lives of Milwaukee’s children and their families.” She said she felt “without any hesitation” that there had been “substantial compliance” with the terms of monitoring. Connecticut similarly exited its decades of monitoring in March 2022, following organizational and operational changes that “dramatically improved” how the state serves children and families. There were also practice and policy implementations “designed to ensure that these improvements will be sustained,” attorneys wrote in the joint motion to end monitoring. Michigan struggling to meet goals In June, Michigan asked a federal judge to end its federal oversight, even though it fell short on most performance measures detailed in the monitors’ most recent report.Donate Failures included an increase in the rate of children abused or neglected while in state care, which monitors wrote “represents an urgent safety threat to children.” Despite struggles to meet the federal benchmarks, most Michigan children in foster care are safe, according to an expert the state hired as part of the case. In court filings, attorneys for the state wrote that the process was at first beneficial to Michigan and the children it serves. However, 18 years in, the “antiquated decree” is causing “institutional paralysis” and the nearly $3 million spent last year on federal court monitors would better serve children and families if it went toward hiring more child welfare professionals. Related: Michigan has spent $40M trying to fix foster care. Abuse is increasing Michigan foster kids struggle under system that gives ‘nothing’ after aging out Michigan under pressure to end ‘orphan tax’ on benefits for foster youth Unlike in Wisconsin and Connecticut, Children’s Rights is opposed to the end of Michigan’s monitoring. Samantha Bartosz, an attorney for the group, commended the progress Michigan has made to this point, but wrote in response to the request to end monitoring that it was premature to do so and the request didn’t stem from any significant change in the facts or law. “It instead rests on (Michigan’s) growing impatience over the practical reality that the consent decree has proven difficult and inconvenient to honor,” she wrote. “Difficulty or inconvenience in implementation do not legally justify the modification of a consent decree.” The most recent monitoring report for Michigan, filed in July, shows the state fell short in 19 of the 24 performance areas tracked, including: The rate of children abused or neglected while in state care, which has been over the federal benchmark since 2023 Efforts to find relative caregivers, often called kinship care, to prevent siblings from being separated in foster care Oversight of and background checks for kinship care placements Ensuring children don’t spend extended periods of time in emergency or temporary facilities Early and continued meetings with biological parents with a goal of reunification with children In a June court filing, Michigan asked a federal judge to end long-running oversight of its child welfare system even though it had not met most benchmarks for improvement. (Asha Lewis / Bridge Michigan) Child welfare monitoring often lasts decades Federal monitoring of child welfare systems through consent decrees is common around the country, as is the often decades-long length of oversight. In fact, Michigan said in its summer motion to end its 18-year monitoring that the average length of such consent decrees is 20 years. Sarah Font, a researcher at Washington University in St. Louis, said the length of Michigan’s monitoring isn’t uncommon and there are states that have been under such agreements for longer. “It’s pretty hard to get out of one once you’ve gotten into it,” she said. “What you’ve seen is a few other states in the last decade have started to challenge the suits and get them dismissed.” She added that there’s no definitive evidence that monitoring is the best path to reform a system, and that states can have difficulty meeting benchmarks because of the large number of performance measures tracked and the high rates of compliance that are required. For example, Font said a state could hire more workers in order to meet a performance measure for staffing or caseloads, but that doesn’t ensure the state will get great work. She added that more workers with better training and resources can result in better investigations, which could increase the rate of substantiated incidents of abuse or neglect of children in state care and move a state further from a crucial exit provision. An evidentiary hearing on Michigan’s motion to end its federal monitoring is scheduled for early December. US District Court Judge Susan DeClercq will then decide whether the state has made enough progress to end the oversight that, as of this summer, has cost at least $40 million. Matt Mencarini is a Report for America corps member who covers data and accountability for Bridge Michigan.

articles.title: Detroit's vacant housing numbers have improved dramatically. But more work remains, study says
articles.description: In 2014, Detroit had more than 114,000 vacant housing units. The think tank Detroit Future City has issued a new report on today's numbers and the long-term trends.
articles.content: Two of the three vacant duplexes the Osborn Neighborhood Alliance renovated and sold for the Mapleridge Street Duplex Project.(City of Detroit)Vacant and abandoned properties, both industrial and residential, have often been held up as symbols of economic struggles in Detroit. And their elimination, in the form of blight removal, have been celebrated by some as a sign of progress.The amount of vacant housing has shrunk dramatically in the past dozen years, but there are still many, many unoccupied units. The think tank Detroit Future City has published a new report that looks at the long-term trends in vacant housing in Michigan’s largest city.Edward Lynch is the director of research at Detroit Future City. He spoke with Morning Edition host Doug Tribou.Doug Tribou: Let's go back to Detroit's housing vacancy problem at its peak. Where did things stand in 2014 and how were the numbers affecting the city at that time?Edward Lynch: According to the American Community Survey, there were about 114,000 or so vacant units at that time. It was something that really affected every neighborhood in the city around that time, too. You have things like the Blight Removal Task Force in a really big push by the city to start to get a handle on the vacant housing units that were kind of all over the place.DT: Detroit Future City analyzed data, as you mentioned, from the American Community Survey, which shows that the number of vacant housing units has fallen by nearly 40% since 2014. So [the total is] now at about 70,000 units as of last year. That's a big decline — 44,000 vacant housing units that are no longer vacant or are gone. What are the factors that led to that drop?EL: There's a couple of things going on. Once we talked about the blight removal and demolition that has gone on and the number of houses that have been demolished throughout the city. I think one thing that we don't talk a lot about is, you know, there's more people here. And so as that number has kind of gone up, you have the combination of more occupied housing units, but also a big portion of that is the demo that's going on over the past 15 years.DT: Well, as you mentioned, Detroit's population has been growing slowly over the last three years. The city has added several thousand people each year. Is the population growing enough that the demand for housing will keep up with the number of units that could reenter the market? And maybe more broadly, is that heading toward a healthy housing rate?EL: Yeah. In some neighborhoods, you're definitely seeing that. The household sizes have been shrinking, but we're seeing a kind of slow and steady growing number of households. There are neighborhoods around the city that do have really low levels of vacancy, but it is a slow and steady path back.DT: Back in 2021, the American Community Survey expanded the categories they use to understand why housing units are unoccupied. Previously, empty housing units that were not actively in the housing market — either up for sale or for rent — were largely chalked up as abandoned. What do the new categories tell us about Detroit's housing picture?EL: So we now know we have about 9,000 units around the city that are currently being renovated. Another 2,900 that are being prepared to sell or rent. We have this pipeline that's been moving. We're kind of moving these housing units back towards being occupied again.DT: How does the situation in Detroit compare to some other cities, either in the Midwest or across the US?EL: Out of the top 50 cities by population, Detroit still has the highest level of vacancy of any of those cities. But the housing units outside of the housing market are really kind of that story and really, what's driving that. For units in the market, those are in line with the national numbers. Some vacancy is a good thing. You want vacant units sometimes, so new people can come in. You can do renovations to them. So this is kind of the, the natural churn of the housing market that you do have kind of these vacant units that serve an active purpose. And that's what these two vacancy rates are trying to capture.DT: After writing this report, what do you see in the numbers in terms of a longer view for what it all means for the city of Detroit?EL: I think it's kind of really important to take the long view. What we're talking about is a city that had 60 years of decline, and now we've kind of turned the ship around. And things are starting to improve. That said, why you take the long view is because if you just look at the numbers, we know that we still have a long way to go.Editor's note: Some quotes in this article have been edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full interview near the top of this page.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed Said Something About Ted Cruz That We’ve All Been Thinking for Years
articles.content: Abdul El-Sayed, Democrat of Michigan, is already more interesting than the average senator-elect. For example, to The Wall Street Journal, he said the nicest thing another senator ever has said about Senator Ted Cruz.El-Sayed, during his interview with The Wall Street Journal, offered a glimpse of how he plans to navigate the Senate alongside some of his fiercest Republican critics. They include Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who during the campaign called El-Sayed “a jihadist” and warned that “Americans will die” if El-Sayed were elected. El-Sayed is the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate.“He’s an a—hole,” El-Sayed said of Cruz. “But if he’s the a—hole from Texas with whom I have to work, I’ll work with the a—hole from Texas. I’ll still call him an a—hole. But if we’re going to get some things done, let’s get some things done.”Not since then senator Al Franken once said, “I like Ted Cruz more than most of my other colleagues like Ted Cruz. And I hate Ted Cruz,” has anyone said anything as complimentary about the Tailgunner.As the WSJ points out, El-Sayed has hit the ground running.Incoming Michigan Democratic Sen. Abdul El-Sayed is emerging as one of his party’s most disruptive forces after helping propel a challenge to Senate leadership that is gaining steam. The outspoken former public health official was among the first to publicly call on Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen to run against New York Sen. Chuck Schumer for the party’s top leadership post when he did so in April. About half a dozen Democratic senators have now publicly endorsed Van Hollen’s long-shot bid, including most recently Sen. Elissa Slotkin, El-Sayed’s more centrist Democratic counterpart from Michigan. They will vote December 1.El-Sayed’s pressure on Schumer suggests he will shift his party’s traditional alliances in ways that unsettle both sides of the aisle. His victory in Michigan, where he ran on an unabashedly progressive platform in a battleground state that President Trump carried twice, has handed him a national stage to push an agenda that includes sweeping changes to healthcare, campaign finance and U.S. foreign aid.Moreover, he has deftly armored himself against the incoming Republican minority’s attempt to turn him into their primary Scary Monster. He’s done that by confounding them.Asked about working with El-Sayed, Cruz said he would “work with anyone who’s doing positive things for America” while reiterating claims he aired during the campaign that El-Sayed supported the Muslim Brotherhood, a charge El-Sayed has denied. Cruz declined to comment on El-Sayed’s characterization of him.In recent interviews, other Senate Republicans were divided on whether they could find common ground with the Michigan freshman. Florida Sen. Rick Scott said that El-Sayed’s push for Medicare-for-All would “destroy the Medicare program.” Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno, the chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee who during the campaign said El-Sayed “should be nowhere near Washington,” said Friday that he had called to congratulate the Democrat on his victory. The pair busted each other’s chops about the college football rivalry between Michigan and Ohio State, and Moreno said he could envision working with El-Sayed on policies supporting U.S. automakers and other efforts to lower costs. “We’ll see what kind of senator he wants to be,” Moreno said. Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy, who campaigned alongside El-Sayed’s opponent Mike Rogers and suggested El-Sayed “sleeps in a bin Laden jersey,” said he had no problem working with the incoming Democrat.Sometimes, in the life of a senator, it becomes necessary to work with the assholes. I’m sure that’s in the Federalist papers somewhere.

articles.content: NEW YORK (WABC) -- Mayor Zohran Mamdani said on Monday that he will have surgery on his Achilles tendon on Friday morning. Mamdani hobbled into a news conference on Friday morning in a boot and crutches after tearing his Achilles in a friendly game of soccer with the press corps. The mayor, who just recently turned 35, said he suffered a non-contact injury while running for a ball on the indoor turf in the second half. He admitted that he did not stretch before the game. On Monday, the mayor announced his plans to have surgery later in the week on Friday. "I'll be down from 9 a.m. to about 2 p.m.," he estimated. "I'm going to be laid out for probably a couple days." First Deputy Mayor Dean Fuleihan will be mayor during Mamdani's surgery on Friday.

articles.title: Michigan schools face librarian shortage, widening gaps in student resources
articles.description: Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools have a trained librarian, limiting students’ access to books and information literacy. A statewide survey aims to document the shortage and guide solutions.
articles.content: This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article. Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools report having a school library staffed with a trained school librarian. Although Michigan strongly recommends that schools employ certified librarians, the state does not require them. In the 2023–24 school year, the state ranked 46th in the student-to-librarian ratio, with one school librarian for every 2,760 students. The lack of school librarians impacts students across Michigan, but particularly in low-income communities like Detroit and Flint and more isolated ones like Alcona County in the northern Lower Peninsula and Ontonagon in the Upper Peninsula, exacerbating disparities in resources for young people. We are scholars in library and information sciences from Wayne State University, studying information access and ethics and equity in education and school libraries. Currently, we are conducting a statewide campaign to contact every school in Michigan and learn about their libraries, staffing, book collections, technology resources and more. Related: Legal battle erupts between Michigan school librarian, activist parent As Michigan scrambles to improve literacy, school librarians are losing their jobs To fix Michigan schools, experts urge better reading skills, less politics Michigan’s 2025–26 School Aid budget funded our statewide survey to measure the school librarian shortage and guide efforts to address it. Our work, and the work of many others, reveals how school librarians help students become strong readers and informed citizens. Catalysts for student achievement A missing librarian is harder to see than an empty bookshelf. A room full of books can look like a school library. But if students cannot borrow those books, teachers have no librarian to plan lessons with, and no one leads author visits or digital citizenship lessons, the space offers only a fraction of what a school library can provide. School librarians bring those services to life. Also called school library media specialists, they hold a teaching certificate and complete advanced education. They connect students with books they want to read and work with teachers to build richer lessons, using library resources to extend learning beyond the textbook. Their impact stretches far beyond standardized test scores, though studies link strong library programs with higher student achievement and improved student literacy, especially for struggling readers. They can instill a love of reading and teach technological skills, which is critical in the age of artificial intelligence. Donate At our Michigan School Census symposium held in 2026, Michigan school librarians and a principal described what that work looks like. Brian Peck, a teacher librarian at Detroit’s UPrep Academy, helped students research and build a library where none had existed. He reported that 334 students voluntarily visited and checked out books during the previous school year. At West Ottawa, librarian Julia Reynolds described replacing crowded shelves with displays that let children see book covers. Circulation quadrupled, she reported. A principal on the panel explained how district support helped schools make library visits a priority from the first week of school. Students’ information worlds Access to information is only a start. Students also need help making sense of what reaches them through searches, social media and AI. AI can create convincing fake videos of students doing or saying things they never did, harming their reputations and undermining trust in what people see online. Less visible forces shape students’ information worlds, too. Algorithms and online platforms often dictate which search results and suggested videos appear first. Students need to understand that the first result is not necessarily the most credible or trustworthy source. AI is becoming so prominent that even elementary school students are learning about it. Building information literacy Information literacy means knowing how to find, judge and use information. School librarians turn those skills into practice. For a history assignment, a librarian might help students compare a newspaper account with a firsthand record. Who produced each source? What might explain their different accounts? The same habits apply to AI. Students can trace a claim to its source, check whether the source exists and compare what it says with the generated answer. A confident response still needs evidence. Guided by certified school librarians, students can build upon these foundations and learn to effectively find, evaluate and use information, including news articles about a historic event for a social studies assignment or to analyze current social media trends. Students can also judge the accuracy, recency and relevance of information. They learn to apply information in decision-making, writing and other forms of communication. Becoming savvy digital citizens Knowing whether information is trustworthy is an important skill. Deciding what to do with it is another. Digital citizenship includes deciding whether to post someone’s photo, seeking their permission before doing so, and choosing not to share a fake video. Recent research emphasizes that digital citizenship prepares students to be empowered online and act ethically, safely and legally in digital environments. Our work also starts with the knowledge young people bring to school. Project Restoring Urban School Libraries helped classroom teachers earn the additional endorsement needed to become school librarians. The program combined mentoring with coursework that drew on students’ cultures, including using hip-hop to explore how young people find, create and share information. Students start by examining the media they already use. A lesson might ask them to trace a sample, credit its creator and discuss what changes when someone else’s work reaches a new audience. Fighting for recognition Principal preparation programs can help school leaders understand what school librarians contribute beyond book checkout. But principals and school librarians often train in separate academic units: colleges of education and schools of library and information science. Without shared coursework or joint projects, principals may complete their training without learning how to work with a school librarian. In our “Closing the Literacy Gap” symposium, we brought school librarians and administrators together on a panel to show what their partnerships make possible. West Ottawa Principal Audra Bolhuis joined school librarian Julia Reynolds and compared a librarian to “an instructional coach.” She described someone teachers can turn to for resources and help with classroom projects, extending the librarian’s role beyond students’ scheduled library visits. School library jobs remain vulnerable to budget cuts, and the number of school librarians across the state has been decreasing since 2010. To understand what schools provide and where support is missing, we launched the state-funded Michigan School Census in September 2026. By Oct. 21, 1,054 schools – about one-third of those invited – had completed it. Our public response map tracks participation across districts. Schools without libraries or librarians are essential to painting the full picture: Their staff can explain how students get books and research help when those services are absent. The findings will guide recommendations for staffing, resources and funding. Counting what schools have is the first step toward deciding what every Michigan student should be able to count on.
