Taliban forest patrols crack down on illegal logging to protect against flooding in Afghanistan
articles.content: CHALAS, Afghanistan (AP) — Deep in the mountains of eastern Afghanistan, a police unit is on patrol. In military fatigues and with automatic rifles slung over their shoulders, the men clamber up steep slopes and trek through deep ravines for days. They belong to the Green Units, a special task force established by the Taliban government to safeguard Afghanistan’s last remaining forests. From the air, vast swaths of land appear devoid of vegetation. Ridge after barren ridge, Afghanistan’s mountains stretch into the distance, hues of brown unbroken by any hint of green. Four decades of war, climate change, uncontrolled logging and timber smuggling have decimated its forests, sometimes resulting in deadly flooding and landslides. The most severe deforestation occurred between the Soviet invasion in 1979 and the fall of the first Taliban regime in 2001, when Afghanistan lost an estimated 50% of its forests, said Mohammad Nasir Shalizi, research assistant professor at North Carolina State University’s Department of Forestry and Wildlife Resources. Much of that was due to illegal logging and timber smuggling, particularly of high-value oak, cedar and other conifers in the eastern provinces, while war, fires and a heavy reliance on wood for heating, cooking and construction also played a part, according to the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization. Climate change, agricultural growth, construction and mining also contributed. Centuries ago, forests covered about 5% of what is now Afghanistan, while woodland dominated by pistachios, almonds and junipers covered around 33%, the FAO said. Currently, forests and shrubland account for just 2.8%. Afghanistan is among the nations most vulnerable to climate change caused mainly by the burning of gas and oil, and among the least prepared to adapt, according to the U.N. Deforestation is something Afghanistan can ill afford. Afghan officials were invited to attend the U.N.’s climate summit, COP31 in Turkey, as observers for the second since the Taliban came to power. Sparse tree cover is already raising temperatures in Afghanistan, said Abdul Hadi Achakzai, head of the Environmental Protection Training and Development Organization, a nongovernmental organization focused on climate change adaptation and ecology in Afghanistan. Tree roots help to prevent soil erosion, so deforestation can have deadly consequences in Afghanistan, where avalanches and flood-triggered landslides often claim hundreds of lives. With climate change driving frequent extreme weather events, forest regeneration is critical. The Aga Khan Foundation has several forest-planting projects in Afghanistan’s mountains, prioritizing areas where communities live below treeless slopes. The projects are essentially “disaster-proofing the communities,” said Apoorva Oza, the foundation’s global program lead for agriculture and climate change. It’s “not only a livelihood or an environmental thing,” Oza said. “It is actually a life-saving intervention.” Successive governments in Afghanistan have backed efforts to safeguard the remaining trees and regenerate lost woodland. Both the current government and the previous U.S.-backed one enforced laws to protect forests and supported tree-planting efforts. The rate of deforestation has slowed considerably in the past two decades, and there are indications that forests are slowly returning in some areas, Shalizi said. After the Taliban seized power in 2021, it created the forest patrol units. And in the five years since, authorities have planted around 126 million seedlings and cuttings, according to Sher Mohammad Hatami, spokesperson for the Ministry of Agriculture, Irrigation and Livestock. Mohammad Halim Rafi, spokesperson for Afghanistan’s National Statistics and Information Authority, said forest cover has increased by 427,000 hectares (1.06 million acres) over the past 15 years. But Shalizi, who was also on the faculty of Kabul University’s Forestry and Natural Resources department from 2009 to 2015, cautioned that the planting won’t necessarily result in healthy forest regeneration. “They plant trees, they have those numbers, but they do not come back and check how many of those trees that they planted survive,” he said. “Usually … the mortality rate is very high.” The main threat forests now face is gradual degradation from mismanagement, such as allowing livestock to graze on saplings, Shalizi said. A forest patrol “helps with the deforestation, like a direct deforestation or material cutting of trees. But it’s not going to help with degradation.” The eastern province of Kunar, bordering Pakistan, is one of the few parts of Afghanistan where sizable forests remain. A bone-jarring three-hour drive along a rough dirt road through the mountains leads to one of the areas where Green Units patrol to prevent the illegal logging of pine, oak and cedar trees. “I can now provide full assurance regarding our forests: no one in Kunar is currently able to cause them any harm,” said Sgt. Khair Ul Rahman, who at 22 has been with a Green Unit for five years. Each 10-man unit patrols for around 10 to 12 days at a time, often working alongside locals who know the mountains well. Countrywide, about 1,000 men serve in forest patrols, said Hatami from the Agriculture Ministry. For Master Sgt. Mohammad Naeem, Kunar is far removed from his home province of Helmand, a largely desert region in southern Afghanistan. “Forests possess great beauty, which is why I came here,” said Naeem, who has been serving in Kunar for two years. “I am very happy in my role here, surrounded by all this beauty.” Cutting down live trees is strictly prohibited, and even felling dead ones requires a permit, explained Kunar police command spokesperson Maj. Faridullah Dehqan. Humans “have a vital need for oxygen and clean air, a need that can be met solely and exclusively by forests,” he said. “Therefore, the protection and preservation of forests are of great importance, and it is a duty incumbent upon all of us to protect them.” While the previous U.S.-backed Afghan government also strictly controlled logging, a lucrative wood-smuggling trade still flourished across the Pakistan border. Authorities say their crackdown has curbed that smuggling. The Green Units also are involved in community outreach and education. That includes explaining a hunting ban to encourage wildlife to return, said Rahman with the Kunar unit. “We visit forested areas, gather people together and speak to them about the importance of forests and the harmful consequences of cutting down trees,” he explained, saying the public awareness campaign is not just a directive from Kabul but also in line with the teachings of the Prophet Muhammad. “In an Islamic society,” he said, “obeying such directives is a mandatory duty.” The Associated Press’ climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. articles.title: FDA Approves First New Hormone Therapy for Early-Stage Breast Cancer in More Than 20 Years
articles.description: The FDA today approved Wilserdly (giredestrant), used alone after surgery in adults with estrogen receptor–positive, HER2-negative breast cancer — the most common subtype of the disease.
articles.content: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Wilserdly (giredestrant), used alone after surgery in adults with estrogen receptor–positive, HER2-negative breast cancer — the most common subtype of the disease. A once-daily oral tablet, Wilserdly is the first new hormone therapy for early-stage breast cancer in more than 20 years. Wilserdly belongs to a class of medicines called oral estrogen receptor antagonists. In estrogen receptor–positive breast cancer, estrogen binds to receptors (proteins) on cancer cells and signals them to grow. Estrogen receptor antagonists like Wilserdly block this process and break down the receptors, cutting off a key driver of tumor growth. “Like many Americans, I have seen breast cancer affect my own family. That experience makes the work we do at FDA deeply personal,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “Even as we recognize how far treatment has come for early-stage breast cancer, the Trump administration knows that patients and their families are counting on us to keep building on that progress, and that’s what we’ve done with today’s approval.” The approval covers adults with estrogen receptor–positive, HER2-negative, stage I, II, or III disease with an intermediate to high risk of recurrence following surgery. Breast cancer is the second most common cancer among women in the United States. An estimated 321,910 new cases are expected in women and 2,670 in men in 2026, approximately 70% of which are estrogen receptor–positive and HER2-negative. “For patients with early-stage hormone-driven breast cancer, the goal after surgery is to keep the cancer from coming back,” said Angelo de Claro, M.D., director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence. “Our review focused on whether Wilserdly could reduce that risk more effectively than the hormone therapies patients already receive. The evidence showed that it could, supporting today’s approval of a new option for patients at intermediate to high risk of recurrence.” In the randomized, multicenter lidERA Breast Cancer trial (NCT04961996), 4,170 adults with this subtype at intermediate to high risk of recurrence were assigned to receive Wilserdly or standard of care hormone therapy — tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor (anastrozole, letrozole, or exemestane) for up to 5 years. Wilserdly reduced the risk of invasive breast cancer recurrence or death by 30% compared with standard hormone therapy (140 versus 196 patients experienced an event during follow-up). This made lidERA the first phase III trial to demonstrate a benefit with an oral estrogen receptor antagonist in early-stage breast cancer. At 3 years, 92.4% of patients taking Wilserdly were alive and free of invasive breast cancer, compared with 89.6% of those taking standard hormone therapy. This translates to about 28 more patients out of every 1,000 alive and free of invasive breast cancer at 3 years. Patients receiving Wilserdly also had a lower risk of cancer returning in another part of the body. Patients are being followed to determine whether Wilserdly helps them live longer. The applicant has agreed to submit these results to the FDA as a postmarketing commitment. The FDA previously approved Wilserdly on November 16, 2026, in combination with everolimus for certain adults with estrogen receptor–positive, HER2-negative, ESR1-mutated advanced or metastatic breast cancer whose disease recurred or progressed during or after prior endocrine therapy. That approval was based on the evERA Breast Cancer trial (NCT05306340). The most common side effects (≥10%) of Wilserdly are muscle and joint pain, hot flashes, tiredness, headache, nausea, slower-than-normal heart rate, dizziness, numbness or tingling in the hands and feet. Common blood test changes include increased liver enzymes, lower blood counts, high blood fat levels, and changes in mineral levels and kidney test results. Wilserdly may harm a developing baby if taken during pregnancy. Women who have not completed menopause should also receive an additional hormone-suppressing medicine with Wilserdly. Men may also receive this medicine, as determined by their healthcare provider. The FDA’s evaluation of the application was supported by an Assessment Aid voluntarily submitted by the applicant. The FDA granted Priority Review to the application. The approval was granted to Genentech, Inc, a member of the Roche Group. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products.

Commentary: Whether ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke
articles.description: Patricia Smith, University of Michigan “Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people. The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic […]
articles.content: A ‘Saturday Night Live’ parody commercial delivered a sobering message to America about a widespread problem. Alican Lazutti/iStock via Getty Images Plus Patricia Smith, University of Michigan “Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people. The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister. “Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains. I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story. A growing trend One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes. My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults. The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion. The “Sister” sketch on “Saturday Night Live” has launched a national conversation about caregiving. Warning: ‘Sister’ may break down Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price. Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people. That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.” Family caregivers pay a price Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour, totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460. But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones. Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits. Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one. AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities. ‘Sister’ lampoons gender roles in caring for aging family members. NBC A ‘daughterhood penalty’ Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “daughterhood penalty,” or tax. Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability. Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives. But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing. Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores. Patricia Smith, Professor of Economics Emeritus, University of Michigan. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. With a speech to text API, you can add audio transcription features to the apps and systems you’re already using. These APIs have use cases across a wide range of industries. They’re helpful for transcribing customer service calls, subtitling videos, taking meeting notes, or even creating clinical documentation. With so many speech to text APIs available to choose from, the best option for your organization will depend on your goals. Some teams prioritize high accuracy rates or low latency, while others value multilingual support. Here’s what to consider when choosing a speech to text API for your project. Speech to text accuracy rates can vary depending on the quality of the underlying audio, so the API may not consistently reach its benchmark scores. Instead of relying entirely on benchmarks to make your decision, test the API using real-world speech that’s appropriate for your planned use case. As you test the API, monitor the word error rate to determine if the output is accurate enough for your needs. You’ll also want to weigh accuracy against cost to decide which API is right for you. If you’re in a highly regulated industry like healthcare, law, or finance, you might prefer to pay more for an API that can deliver consistently high accuracy rates, regardless of audio quality. However, if your budget is limited, you might choose to sacrifice some accuracy for affordability. Another factor to consider when choosing your speech to text API is latency, or the length of the delay between the audio and the transcription. When evaluating API options, run a latency test with real-world call conditions, instead of just transcribing sample audio. This is a particularly important consideration if you’re using the API to transcribe meetings or customer calls in real time. If the latency is too high, the model will transcribe speech much slower than it actually happens, resulting in a poor user experience. On top of that, you’ll also need to consider the API’s overall reliability. Professional speech to text tools often need to transcribe multiple audio files at the same time. The most reliable APIs can handle several projects concurrently without sacrificing accuracy or latency. While reliable performance is essential for an audio transcription API, you’ll also need to consider your budget. If your budget is limited, you’ll need to find an API that balances consistency and affordability. Speech to text APIs are often priced per-character, per-word, or per-minute of audio transcribed. Some APIs also charge a flat monthly subscription rate, while others allow you to pay as you go. Your API provider might offer volume discounts, which can help keep costs in check if you’re transcribing at scale. However, most plans also have monthly subscription limits, and you could end up paying overage fees if you exceed them. When choosing an API, consider how discounts and limits could affect your total monthly spend. When evaluating pricing, think about how many files you need to transcribe each month and if you plan on scaling up in the future. If you’re transcribing a large volume of audio, you may need to sacrifice some accuracy to keep costs in check. Infrastructure costs are another important consideration if you’re transcribing audio at scale. Many businesses consider self-hosting with an open-source transcription model to cut back on costs. However, if you go this route, you’ll need to pay for and maintain your own digital infrastructure, which could end up costing more than an API. With a managed speech to text API, you’re not paying hosting and storage costs for your speech to text projects. If your business has an international presence or multilingual customer base, you’ll need a speech to text API that supports all the languages you do business in. When comparing your API options, review the number of languages currently available, then do a test for each of the languages you want to transcribe. Then, evaluate the API’s performance for each test. The transcription model should deliver similar accuracy and latency across each language. Even if your business currently operates in just one language, you may need multilingual support in the future. When choosing a multilingual speech recognition API, consider your long-term plans and whether you might expand to other countries as you grow. Before committing to an API, make sure it meets your industry’s compliance standards and data privacy standards for the country and state you’re operating in. If your speech to text API isn’t compliant, it could introduce security and privacy risks for both your business and your customers. First, check to see what data the API retains and how long it keeps that data on file. You’ll also need to consider where the API provider is storing this data and what the local data laws are in that country if it’s different than your own. You’ll also need to make sure the API provider has strong cybersecurity practices to protect your data from threat actors. If you’re in a highly regulated industry, you’ll also need to make sure that the API provider has the appropriate certifications and internal security measures for industry compliance. For example, if you’re using a speech to text API for clinical documentation in the United States, the API needs to be HIPAA-compliant. If you’re using speech to text specifically to transcribe and analyze customer service calls, there are additional considerations to make when choosing an API. These include: Speech to text APIs work best when they have clean audio to work with. When possible, record your audio in a quiet room with a high-quality microphone so every word is clear and crisp. However, recording in this environment isn’t always possible. If you have to record without a microphone or record in an area with lots of background noise, you can use a voice isolator to clean it up before transcribing it. A voice isolator can remove street sounds, background conversations, ambient noise, or mic feedback so speech sounds clearer. Scribe also has built-in background audio filtering for real-time streams, but a voice isolator is still worth using on very noisy pre-recorded files. If your conversations contain company names, product names, or industry jargon, use keyterm prompting to provide the correct spelling and improve speech to text accuracy. PostNord partnered with ElevenLabs to replace it entirely: the previous system was fully decommissioned in roughly 90 days, with task completion rising from 45% to 60%. PostNord’s previous phone support solution was AI-based, yet it plateaued at about 45% of calls resolved without escalation. For a team that had adopted AI voice before most of the industry, a plateau was the signal to move again. To improve its success rate, the PostNord team wanted a system that could speak more natural Swedish, resolve more of the most common inquiries, and be tuned continuously in production. Built on ElevenAgents, the new system uses an orchestrator that identifies the need of each customer and routes it to one of four specialized subagents. This includes a dedicated tracking agent that keeps the most common enquiry types on lighter, cheaper footprints. Task completion rose from 45% to 60%, with an agent that could: PostNord’s agent architecture includes guardrails, an intent classifier, subagents, and edge conditions, as well as A/B testing infrastructure that splits live traffic between model configurations so the team can keep optimizing in production. With that refinement loop, the team believes the agent’s completion rate will keep climbing. Every configuration change is tested against live calls, so they see the current 60% figure as a current reading, not the final metric. The ElevenAgents platform brought industry-leading voice, natural turn-taking, and orchestration together in one platform, giving us the foundation to deliver a far more natural experience for callers at enterprise scale. Both teams reviewed every component and analyzed the prior phase's calls before each go/no-go decision. More natural conversation in Swedish was one of the reasons PostNord wanted a new system, and getting it right over a real phone network took work on three fronts: PostNord had deep domain expertise — their customers, call flows, and SIP infrastructure — what they needed was a partner on the AI architecture side. Detroit schools increase police presence amid rise in after-school fights
articles.description: DPSCD is increasing police presence at Mumford while community violence intervention groups push for more investment in prevention programs.
articles.content: Amid escalating violence, Detroit’s public school district has increased police presence at at least one high school and implemented a plan to address the culture. Detroit Public Schools Community District Superintendent Nikolai Vitti said more officers are in place at Mumford High School and a faculty plan is also in place as the neighborhood high school and some others experience a rise in large after-school fights. Vitti provided the information during a Nov. 10 school board meeting in response to questions from DPSCD Board President LaTrice McClendon who sought an update on what the district was doing to ensure student safety. Parent and advocate Melissa Redman said during public comment that fights at Mumford are problematic and happening almost every day inside and outside the school. “At one point, Mumford High School was the place to be. We must take control of what happens here,” Redman told the board. “I went to Mumford, I still support Mumford. I live in this community, and I’m a person that will speak up about it.” The superintendent did not specify beyond Mumford which schools are seeing increased violence, but a parent from Thurgood Marshall Elementary-Middle School also spoke during the meeting, saying that her daughter was being bullied and having her life threatened by students. The parent also noted that a weapon made its way into the school despite the building’s metal detectors and students having to carry clear backpacks. “I wanna know what procedures are actually being taken,” the parent said. Vitti acknowledged that the district was aware of the incident with the weapon at Thurgood Marshall and said that it was under investigation. DPSCD Chief of Public Safety Labrit Jackson said he did not know about the incident at Thurgood Marshall or increased violence in other district schools. Fights, he said, are usually dealt with at the school level. “Not every fight rises to the level of public safety involvement,” Jackson told BridgeDetroit, “so we wouldn’t be apprised of every fight that happens in a school.” School safety and security has been top of mind for DPSCD this year. In June, the board adopted a $1.1 billion budget for the 2026-27 school year, where funds were allocated for the expansion of security guards and police officers and new metal detectors at neighborhood high schools, Martin Luther King Jr. Senior High School and large K-8 schools after two 2025 incidents involving students bringing weapons to the classroom. The district this year also received a surplus of $10.3 million in one-time state mental health and school safety funds. Representatives from some of Detroit’s Community Violence Intervention (CVI) groups also attended the Nov. 10 meeting, including Team Pursuit Executive Director Quincy Smith. The organization works out of the 48205 ZIP code on Detroit’s east side and provides programming at Denby and Osborne high schools and at Fisher Magnet Academy. Smith said CVI groups can help support the district’s safety initiatives. “We have credible messengers, neighborhood influencers and individuals who live in the community who have relationships with those students who can intervene and de-escalate a lot of those situations,” he said. Ciera Renee, director of public health and safety for another CVI group, FORCE Detroit, said she implemented a violence prevention effort at Cody High School called Detroit Keepers. The program offers mentorship, conflict resolution and mental health support to students. Renee asked the board to prioritize sustainable funding for CVI programs within DPSCD schools. Vitti told BridgeDetroit that the district has used its own funding and state grants to support those programs. “Our children deserve to have more than a response after violence occurs,” Renee said. “They deserve intentional systems designed to prevent violence before it reaches the classrooms, homes and neighborhoods.” Jackson said DPSCD partners with seven CVI groups overall. In addition to Team Pursuit and FORCE Detroit, Detroit Friends and Family, Detroit 300 and Ceasefire Detroit are among the CVI partners and “we’re always looking for expansion.” Vitti said that DPSCD also works with the mentoring program Pretty Brown Girl to provide social-emotional learning, academic support and leadership development for girls. The district, he said, has also received a grant to provide male mentoring to students. Sharlonda Buckman, DPSCD’s assistant superintendent of Family and Community Engagement (FACE), told BridgeDetroit the CVI grant is from the Michigan Department of Education, but she didn’t specify the amount. DPSCD’s 2026-27 budget includes increased funding for male mentoring through its FACE department. “In addition to that, we’ve protected schools with extra deans, extra assistant principals, even when enrollment was declining in our neighborhood high schools,” Vitti said during the board meeting. “We’ve increased the allocation for counselors.” Based on feedback he’s received from principals, Vitti said one thing the district needs to improve on is getting students to disperse faster after school dismissal. “That is going to be a responsibility of our police officers and some administrative staff to continue to move students to their bus stops, walking home or getting rides home rather than staying around after school,” Vitti said. Keeping intersections safe During the Nov. 10 discussion, board secretary Monique Bryant said she’s received emails about students who were injured in high traffic areas. “What are we doing that we can get additional crossing guards at some of these heavy intersections?” she asked. There are currently 30 crossing guards across the district, provided by the Detroit Police Department’s Traffic Safety Unit, but the police department has had difficulty hiring more, Vitti said. “What we have done at individual schools is rely on volunteers or police presence at certain schools that have recurring challenges,” he said. Bryant asked if the district is having parent groups work with organizations like Michigan Safe Routes to School (SRTS). The organization creates an action plan and finds grants to implement changes, such as temporary or permanent speed bumps on residential streets, bike lane barriers and long-term initiatives to narrow roadways. Jackson told BridgeDetroit that the district still partners with SRTS. McClendon suggested that the district’s police department assist in managing schools with high traffic areas. Vitti told McClendon that he’s reluctant to shift focus because he wants to ensure that there are enough officers on duty at the schools experiencing high levels of fighting. Member Ida Short raised the prospect of security officers using drones to overlook high traffic areas. Vitti said DPSCD has six drones that are used to enhance safety and security efforts. “Their uses include crowd monitoring at sporting events, asset protection, inspections of elevated or difficult-to-access areas on district properties and aerial searches in support of school safety operations,” he told BridgeDetroit. “When permitted, drones may also be used to help monitor crowds during building evacuations.” Taylor, Dearborn and Sterling Heights are among the metro Detroit police departments using drones to respond faster during emergency calls and to provide information during crimes and traffic crashes. DPD does not currently have an approved policy for drone use.

articles.title: A little-seen change in maternity billing codes could reveal a fuller picture of care
articles.description: For decades, pregnancy has been approached by insurance companies as a singular event, with one payment at the end given to one provider, no matter how many prenatal visits occurred over the months or how straightforward or complex the pregnancy was along the way. Beginning Jan. 1, that approach will change, with the unbundling of […]
articles.content: A change to billing codes for pregnancy-related care beginning Jan. 1 will change the insurance process from one lump-sum payment billed at the end of a full pregnancy to separate services for the first time in 30 years. Providers say it won’t change much for patients, but will have many upsides for the overall provision of maternal care. (Photo by Noelle Straub/Stateline)For decades, pregnancy has been approached by insurance companies as a singular event, with one payment at the end given to one provider, no matter how many prenatal visits occurred over the months or how straightforward or complex the pregnancy was along the way. Beginning Jan. 1, that approach will change, with the unbundling of the codes providers use to bill insurance and receive payment for their services. The five-digit codes are used to describe the type of care a patient received, including specific procedures and testing. While it isn’t expected to change much for patients, providers say it will make it easier to transfer care among clinics and hospitals, ease revenue burdens and perhaps most importantly, provide a more detailed and data-driven picture of maternity care nationwide that is opaque under the current system — though it remains somewhat unclear how private health insurance companies and Medicaid programs will respond to the change. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, known as ACOG, worked with the American Medical Association to develop the new codes, which are then communicated to health insurers, including Medicaid. Pregnancies that began in the 2026 calendar year will likely still be billed under the global code, but those that have their first visit after Jan. 1 will use the new system. Lisa Satterfield, vice president of practice, sustainability and workforce initiatives for ACOG, said the group started working on this change in 2022, after feedback from providers that the system was outdated. “The way they were designed was for one provider to get billed from the very first prenatal visit to the very last postpartum visit,” Satterfield said. “It was not practical anymore.” In the vast majority of cases, nothing should change about how much patients are paying for care, Satterfield said, because maternity visits are considered preventative care under the federal Affordable Care Act and not subject to cost sharing. Patients may just see more statements in the mail with an explanation of their benefits. With the current global payment, no services are billed after the confirmation of a pregnancy until the last postpartum visit, Satterfield said, which leads to a long delay in the revenue from each visit in between. On average, Satterfield said, the global payment from health insurers to OB-GYNs or midwives was about $3,500 for an entire pregnancy, regardless of whether it was a patient with relatively few or no complications along the way, including delivery, or someone who needed many more interventions and had a long, complicated delivery. “It didn’t matter, they got paid the same, regardless of the services that were being provided,” Satterfield said. If patients switch among providers or clinics for various reasons, sometimes a provider isn’t even aware that the patient had seen someone else until the claim is denied, leaving that provider to try to negotiate with the insurer or ask the other provider to share their payment. Many times, it just results in lost revenue for the health providers, she said. The current bundled code also has allowed some insurers to try to lump other services into that same payment, she said, such as the insertion of a birth control implant, which some women opt to do after delivering a baby, that otherwise could be charged separately. Study shows sharp increases in maternal deaths over two decades Dr. Barbra Fisher, a maternal-fetal medicine specialist in central California, said there is a separation of billing if someone is referred to the specialist clinic for various reasons in pregnancy, such as a fetal anomaly or high-risk conditions like gestational diabetes or hypertension. Some specialist clinics use the global code for their services as well, she said, but they also have the option to bill separately for services. The biggest changes will come for standard OB care rather than specialists, she said. But she added there are some concerns among obstetrics providers about how insurers will adjust to the changes, particularly private health insurance. “I think practices are worried because they just don’t know what the reaction is going to be,” Fisher said. “We don’t know what state Medicaid payers and private insurance will do.” Dr. Mark Simon, chief medical officer of the national Ob Hospitalist Group, said the insurance providers he spoke with earlier in the fall didn’t have set plans yet on how they would respond to the changes, so there are still unknowns. But he said he sees many upsides to the changes, including how closely researchers can track the details of obstetrical care and its variations by patient. Maternal mortality rates in the United States remain stubbornly high compared with peer countries. In 2024, the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 17.9 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, compared with 8.4 per 100,000 in Canada and 5.5 in the United Kingdom. That rate in the U.S. also varies significantly by state and race, with a much higher rate of 44.8 deaths per 100,000 births among Black women. Simon said the global payment made it difficult to know how to improve those rates when there was little information about how many times a patient was seen during pregnancy and afterward, what kind of delivery and labor management they had, and what types of providers they saw. “You lose a lot of quality data that you need to help systems improve,” he said. “We’re trying to improve the healthcare system with one hand tied behind our back, because we don’t have full information on what’s actually happening.” The new data will lag behind until 2026 pregnancies are out of the global billing system, he said, but once full data is returned starting late in 2027 and into 2028, Simon thinks there will be many opportunities to make more informed decisions about maternity care. “I’m very hopeful that with this kind of information, we’ll be able to direct efforts to areas where we identify weaknesses, as it were, that were leaving patients behind,” he said. Fisher said she’s looking forward to the change as well. “This has been a long time in the making, and I think it will be much more equitable. I think it will be good for the patients and good for the practices,” she said. Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org. articles.title: Michigan decarbonization road map presents path to reducing manufacturing emissions
articles.description: As state leaders continue work toward mitigating Michigan’s contributions to climate change, the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy has released a policy road map detailing how to cut greenhouse gas emissions in the state’s industrial sector while strengthening manufacturing. Building on the MI Healthy Climate Plan and the state’s Comprehensive Climate Action […]
articles.content: The Ford Rouge Plant in Dearborn on July 7, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)As state leaders continue work toward mitigating Michigan’s contributions to climate change, the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy has released a policy road map detailing how to cut greenhouse gas emissions in the state’s industrial sector while strengthening manufacturing. Building on the MI Healthy Climate Plan and the state’s Comprehensive Climate Action Plan, the road map, prepared by clean energy consultants at 5 Lakes Energy, examines the factors involved in reducing emissions across Michigan’s industrial sector. Manufacturing provides more than 600,000 jobs and contributes $100 billion to the state’s gross domestic product annually, making it a central part of Michigan’s economy. However, industry accounts for 17.5% of the state’s greenhouse gas emissions, with the road map noting that Michigan will need to significantly reduce the amount of industrial emissions if it is to hit its 2050 goal of carbon neutrality. Because Michigan’s industrial sector includes facilities of varying sizes, the road map emphasizes that there is no one-size-fits-all approach to decarbonization. At Michigan climate conference, Inslee says states still hold power on clean energy While targeting decarbonization investments at major industries will allow the state to take a major step toward its goal, the road map notes that small and mid-sized manufacturers will need technical assistance, financing and help implementing these improvements. Although technologies to reduce emissions are available, the road map identifies high upfront costs, energy prices and production risks as major barriers to their adoption. In developing their recommendations, consultants prioritized practical, actionable policies, distinguishing between near-term actions, long-term strategies and efforts that may require additional authority, funding, engagement with utility companies or federal government support. During a Thursday webinar hosted by EGLE, Andrew Hoffmeister, a senior consultant on 5 Lakes Energy’s industry team, noted that the report also focused on four technological pathways facilities can pursue to reduce emissions: energy efficiency, electrification, fuel switching, and carbon capture, utilization and storage. As for its recommendations, the road map suggests eight core policy measures. The first suggestion was to establish recurring grants for industries to modernize and decarbonize their technology. Hoffmeister also recommended the state develop additional financing options to support the grant program. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE To address the ongoing costs of producing clean industrial heat, 5 Lakes Energy also encouraged the state to create a clean heat production tax credit that would help facilities offset the cost difference between electricity and natural gas while incentivizing the use of clean heat technologies. The consulting firm also advised state energy regulators to look into developing an electricity rate structure for industrial facilities using technology that displaces fossil fuels. “Of course, we don’t want those rates to work by shifting costs onto existing customers,” Hoffmeister said. “The objective would be to develop rates that reflect the actual costs of serving those loads and recognize the benefits that manufacturers using those technologies can provide to the system.” While the first few recommendations focused on lowering the cost of lower carbon-producing products, Hoffmeister noted that 5 Lakes’ fourth recommendation was centered on creating a stronger market for those products. By establishing a “Buy Clean, Buy Michigan” program that utilizes the government’s ability to purchase materials, the state can create demand for lower-carbon construction and manufactured materials, the road map explains. Expanding and targeting existing workforce programs to support modernization and industrial decarbonization programs was also a priority. The road map also advocated for an expedited permitting pathway for projects that reduce emissions and improve air quality. Using recycled materials in manufacturing is another way to reduce industrial emissions, Hoffmeister explained, with the road map advising the state to expand its investment into recycling, support the development of a market for these materials and coordinate with the previously suggested “Buy Clean, Buy Michigan” program to create a demand for these materials. In its final recommendation, the road map encourages the state to look into the feasibility of a cap-and-invest program. This would set a limit on the amount of greenhouse gases major industrial facilities can emit in a region while allowing the state to auction emissions allowances. The state can then use that auction revenue to provide funding for industrial decarbonization projects, workforce development, technical assistance or community investments, Hoffmeister explained.
